# Ticket: catalog-db-01 /var at 100%, log agent failing

**Opened:** 2025-01-02 21:25 UTC by DBA on-call
**Severity:** sev3
**Host:** catalog-db-01.prod.internal
**Runbook:** RB-008
**State:** closed

## Description

Log agent errors from catalog-db-01 started arriving at 21:25 over the network: `ENOSPC` each time it tried to save its read position. Nothing local is being written. Postgres still serving. Taking it.

## Comments

**21:31, DBA on-call**
Free space check on the mount: 100% used. `/var` shares the root disk on this VM, so anything that writes to the root filesystem is at risk, not only logs. Checked the database first: a read from `psql` returns normally and the catalog-api error rate is flat. Treating this as sev3, no page to team-catalog yet.

**21:38, DBA on-call**
Sized the directories under it with `du`, sorted. Top entry by a wide margin is `/var/log/journal`. Postgres's own directories are small next to it. No `.gz` pile-up, apt cache tiny.

**21:44, DBA on-call**
`journalctl --disk-usage` agrees: the journal alone accounts for nearly all of the used space. Looked at `/etc/systemd/journald.conf`: every line is still commented out, the file is the distribution default. No `SystemMaxUse` anywhere in it.

**21:52, DBA on-call**
Holding off on deleting anything by hand inside `/var/log/journal`. The runbook path for this case is a vacuum through journald itself. Ran `sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=500M`. It removed archived journal files oldest first and left the active ones.

**21:58, DBA on-call**
`df -h /var` now has plenty of headroom. Log agent resumed: its position writes succeed and it began shipping what it had buffered.

**22:02, DBA on-call**
Before calling the space problem solved, checked for deleted files still held open by a process: `lsof +L1` came back empty. So the journal was the whole story, not one piece of it.

**22:10, DBA on-call**
Making the fix permanent on this host. Added `SystemMaxUse=500M` under `[Journal]` in `/etc/systemd/journald.conf` and restarted `systemd-journald`. `journalctl --disk-usage` after restart is under the cap. This VM did not have the cap before tonight; it does now.

**22:25, DBA on-call**
Checked whether anything failed while the disk was full. Postgres did not log write errors for its data during the window that we can find, and catalog-api showed no change. The only casualties we can name are the log agent's position file and whatever local log lines could not be stored before the vacuum.

**22:40, DBA on-call**
Watching growth. `journalctl --disk-usage` steady. Root disk usage steady.

**23:15, DBA on-call**
Agent backlog fully shipped, usage flat for over half an hour. Closing, 110 minutes after the first error. Open questions below.

## What a reader should know

- The vacuum only removed archived journal files. Recent entries, including everything from tonight after 21:52, are still on the host.
- Local log lines from the first part of the evening may be missing; the agent's buffer covered what it could, but anything written straight to disk while it was full did not survive.
- Postgres was not restarted and nothing in its directories was touched.

## Follow-up

Tonight the first sign came from the log agent complaining about its own position file, over the network. Proposal: alert on that specific agent error, since it fires even when nothing local can be written.
resolution: Vacuumed the journal to 500M, then set SystemMaxUse=500M in /etc/systemd/journald.conf and restarted journald so the limit holds.
root_cause: catalog-db-01 never had a journald size cap, so the systemd journal under /var/log/journal kept growing until the root disk had no room left.
symptoms: The log agent on catalog-db-01 reported ENOSPC on its own writes and /var stood at 100%; Postgres kept answering queries.
title: catalog-db-01 root disk full of journal files

# Card payments failed from midnight on an expired processor certificate, 2025-01-14

payments timeline, sev1, 00:00 to 02:40 UTC.

```
00:00  the certificate that card-processor-proxy presents to the processor passes its end
       date. card-processor-proxy-01 and card-processor-proxy-02 both start logging CPX-E600
       on every outbound call
00:00  payments-api spends 3 attempts on each card payment, then logs PAYAPI-E1107
00:04  payments on-call paged
00:25  the certificate held in the Secret is inspected; its end date is midnight, which
       matches the first error
00:40  request for a replacement certificate goes to the processor
02:30  the replacement arrives
02:38  Secret updated with the new certificate and both proxies restarted
02:40  CPX-E600 stops on both proxies; card payments succeed again
```

## What the first hour looked like

The change was abrupt. The certificate worked until its end date and failed from the next
second, so there was no slow build-up to read and no lead-in on any dashboard. Card payments
were failing from 00:00, and the page arrived four minutes later at 00:04.

Because it was the small hours, traffic was light, yet each pod still logged around 3.5
failures every second. payments-api gave up on a payment after every three of them.

## Waiting on the processor

The certificate comes from the processor, not from our own CA, so nothing could be minted
on our side. Once the end date was confirmed at 00:25, the work was the request at 00:40 and
then the wait until 02:30. The proxy loads the certificate only when it starts, so the
Secret update at 02:38 went together with the restart; the errors were gone two minutes
after that.

## Scope

Both proxies were affected from the same minute, so this was not one bad pod and a restart of
either on its own would have changed nothing. The failure was in the credential both of them
share, and it stayed in place until the replacement was loaded on each.

## Follow-ups

- From 2025-01-15, alerts fire 30 days and 7 days ahead of the certificate's end date.
resolution: A replacement certificate arrived from the processor at 02:30, the Secret was updated and the proxy restarted at 02:38, and the errors stopped at 02:40.
root_cause: The client certificate card-processor-proxy presents to the processor reached its end date at 00:00 UTC and nobody had renewed it.
symptoms: From 00:00 every call from both card-processor-proxy pods to the card processor failed with CPX-E600, and payments-api logged PAYAPI-E1107 for each card payment after its 3 attempts.
title: Processor client certificate lapsed at midnight

# Handoff: slow and failing search, Wednesday 15 January 2025

**search-api-01, search-cluster-02, search-cluster-03 · slow searches and SRCH-E502 · sev3 · 22:30 to 23:40 UTC · RB-003 · closed**

Handing this over finished. Search is back to normal and the open questions are listed below.

## Current state

Search answers at its usual speed and `SRCH-E502` is not appearing in the search-api-01 log. The CPU load on the -02 and -03 cluster nodes is back to ordinary levels. Nothing else is open.

## What the evening looked like

From 22:30 the two cluster nodes named above were busy with CPU, and searches that went through search-api-01 got slow and then began to fail with `SRCH-E502`. The load pointed at one query shape: a pattern that began with a wildcard, aimed at the `title` field. RB-003 lists that shape among the usual causes of a loaded search cluster. The incident ran 70 minutes, from 22:30 to 23:40.

## Who was affected

Callers of search through search-api-01 saw slow answers first and then failures. No customer count was recorded.

## Not recorded

- Who or what sent the query, and from where.
- How many such queries arrived, and whether it was one query repeated or several.
- What was done to stop it. Only the outcome is known: the load had cleared by 23:40.

## Open items

1. Find out whether `search.block_leading_wildcard`, the search-api flag for this pattern, was on that evening, and decide whether it should be.
2. Capture the caller of any repeat from the search-api access log while it is still happening.
resolution: team-catalog handled it; the errors and the extra load were gone by 23:40.
root_cause: An expensive search with a wildcard at the start of the pattern on the title field loaded search-cluster-02, search-cluster-03 and search-api-01; who sent it was not recorded.
symptoms: From 22:30 search-api-01 logged SRCH-E502 while search-cluster-02 and search-cluster-03 ran under heavy CPU and searches slowed.
title: A leading-wildcard title query loaded the search cluster

# Growing template cache: notification-worker-01 killed for memory

sev4 · 2025-01-18 23:40 to 2025-01-19 00:40 UTC · cause: notification-worker · affected: notification-worker-01 · runbook: RB-005

| Time (UTC) | Component | Entry |
|---|---|---|
| 23:40 | notification-worker-01 | Container terminated with `OOMKilled` and restarted. Memory in the new process started low and began to rise again. |
| during the hour | notification-worker-01 | The container was killed again; the times and the number of kills were not kept. |
| 00:40 | notification-worker-01 | No further `OOMKilled`. Incident closed. |

## Cause

The cause was an in-process cache of message templates inside the worker. It grew without a limit, and when the process had taken more memory than the container is allowed, the kernel killed the container. Because the cache lives inside the process, each kill emptied it, which is why a restarted worker began with memory low and then climbed again. That climb-then-kill pattern is the one RB-005 contrasts with a limit that is simply too small for a known peak.

## Effect

The incident is sev4. The worker sends emails through an external provider. How much mail was delayed while the container was cycling was not recorded, and no measure of any queue behind it was kept. The hour from 23:40 to 00:40 is 60 minutes.

## Where it happened

Only notification-worker-01 is named. Its container is the one with the cache, and the kills and restarts happened on that pod. The worker consumes the `notification-worker` group's messages and sends through the provider's HTTP API, so each restart paused that work until the new process came up.

## In-flight work

The worker has up to 20 sends in flight per pod. A kill ends the process with whatever sends were in progress at that moment, and the outcome of those sends is not recorded. Since the number of kills was not kept either, the number of sends affected cannot be estimated from what remains.

## Suggestions

- Give the template cache a size bound or an expiry, so memory flattens instead of climbing.
- Look at the memory history for the worker when it restarts without an obvious job behind it.
resolution: The platform on-call handled it with RB-005; OOMKilled was no longer being recorded for notification-worker-01 by 00:40. What stopped the growth was not noted.
root_cause: An in-process cache of message templates inside notification-worker-01 kept growing with no limit until the container passed its memory limit and the kernel killed it.
symptoms: From 23:40 the container of notification-worker-01 was killed with OOMKilled and restarted; memory climbed again after each restart.
title: Template cache outgrew notification-worker-01

# Ticket: certificate error reported by one client, edge certificate in date

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Severity | sev4 |
| Service | edge-gateway |
| Started | 2025-01-19 13:40 UTC |
| Resolved | 2025-01-19 15:25 UTC |
| Team | team-platform |
| Runbook | RB-025 |

**Description.** A client reports that its device refuses the certificate our edge presents. No one else has reported anything similar.

## Comments

**13:40** · support: ticket opened from the client's report. The refusal happens during the connection itself, before any request is sent.

**13:55** · platform on-call: searched the edge logs from the time of the report. edge-gateway-03 has a handshake that the peer broke off at 13:41, which fits the report and may be the client trying again; nothing in the line says which client it was. New connections are spread evenly over all three edge pods, so another attempt from the same device could reach any of them.

**14:10** · platform on-call: read the certificate that edge-gateway-03 hands out. Its dates are current; it does not run out until 2025-03-16 10:15 UTC, about two months away. The chain is complete. Only this pod was checked. That was enough here, because the question was whether the device or the certificate was at fault, not which pod the device reached.

**14:25** · platform on-call: a certificate that is in date, refused by one device while no other client complains, points at that device. RB-025 lists this case: one client failing while everyone else is fine points at the client's clock, with nothing to change at the edge. A device sees a certificate as expired or not yet valid when its own date falls outside the certificate's dates.

**14:40** · platform on-call: answer sent to support, asking that the client check the date and time on the device.

**15:25** · platform on-call: closing as a client-side fault. No change to the edge.

## Why only edge-gateway-03 is named

The fault sits on the client, not on a pod. A device with a wrong clock refuses a valid certificate whichever pod answers, and the load balancer spreads new connections evenly over the three pods, so the pod named here is chance. edge-gateway-03 appears only because its log holds the broken-off handshake from 13:41 and because it was the pod whose certificate was read. It was not changed.

## Why this stayed at sev4

One client reported a problem, no other client did, and edge-gateway-03 kept serving requests normally throughout. The ticket was handled through support rather than as an outage, and it was open for 105 minutes (13:40 to 15:25).

## Left alone on purpose

- The Secret `edge-public-tls` was not touched. The certificate in it was valid.
- No pod was restarted and no rollout was started. A restart reloads the same file and would not change what the client's device decides.
- No early renewal. The certificate was valid; the fault was the device's clock.

## What this ticket does not record

It does not name the client, say what kind of device it used or quote the exact message the device showed. It also does not record whether the client confirmed the clock fix afterwards; the ticket was closed on the evidence above, not on a reply from the client.
resolution: Nothing was changed at the edge; the ticket was closed as a client-side fault at 15:25.
root_cause: The clock on that client's own device was wrong, so it judged the edge's valid certificate to be outside its validity dates.
symptoms: A single client reported a certificate error when connecting to the edge; edge-gateway-03 logged a handshake ended by the peer, consistent with the report, and no other client reported a problem.
title: One client rejected a valid edge certificate

# Ticket: payment requests timing out at the edge, payments-api pods throttled

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Severity | sev2 |
| Service | payments-api (seen at the edge) |
| Hosts | payments-api-01, payments-api-02 |
| Opened | 2025-01-23 18:10 UTC |
| Closed | 2025-01-23 19:15 UTC (65 minutes) |
| Team | team-platform |
| Runbook | RB-002 |

**Description.** Payment requests are coming back from the edge as `504`. The gateway answers `504` when the upstream has not responded within its 15 second route timeout, and the slow upstream here is payments-api. Both payments-api-01 and payments-api-02 were being throttled on CPU, and the throttling held requests past that timeout.

**Where the symptom shows.** The failing requests are payment calls, which reach payments-api through the route `/v1/payments/*`. The edge is where the error is produced and where customers meet it; the delay itself is inside the two payments-api pods.

**Reading the numbers.** RB-002 counts throttling above about 25% of periods as significant, and says the throttling view of the Grafana "Container CPU" panel is where to see it. This ticket records no throttled-period percentage and no CPU figure, so none is stated.

**Scope.** The ticket covers two hosts, payments-api-01 and payments-api-02, one family of routes, `/v1/payments/*`, and one span of time, from 18:10 to 19:15 on 23 January 2025. Throttling here means the pods were held back by their CPU limit for part of each scheduling period, so requests waited even though the pods were running. RB-002 is the runbook for that condition on payments-api and fraud-scorer.

**Why the edge is in the title.** The edge-gateway pods are not hosts of this incident. They appear because they are where a slow upstream turns into an error: a request that outlasts the route timeout is ended by the gateway, and the caller receives the `504`. Nothing is recorded about the gateway pods themselves being unwell.

**Ownership.** team-platform owns RB-002 and took the ticket. payments-api sets `GOMAXPROCS` from its CPU limit in its Deployment, which is the platform's usual guard against thread counts outrunning the limit.

**Timing.** The ticket was opened as the `504`s began, at 18:10, and closed at 19:15, once they had stopped. The 65 minutes in the table are that gap and nothing else; no figure for the worst minute or the busiest route is on file. The severity was sev2 for the whole span, and no entry changes it.

## Comments

**18:10** · opened. `504`s at the edge on payment requests; payments-api-01 and payments-api-02 throttled on CPU.

**Handling** · team-platform took the ticket. Between the opening and the close no further entry carries a time.

**19:15** · closed. The `504`s had stopped by this time, 65 minutes after the ticket was opened.

## Not in the ticket

- How many payment requests received a `504`.
- The share of throttled periods, and how it moved over the hour.
- What first drew attention to the pods, and who looked at them first.
- The step that ended the throttling.
- Whether either pod restarted during the hour; the ticket is silent on it.
resolution: team-platform took the incident; the 504s had stopped by 19:15.
root_cause: CPU throttling on payments-api-01 and payments-api-02 held requests up past the edge's route timeout, so the gateway answered 504; no throttling figure was recorded.
symptoms: From 18:10 the edge returned 504 on payment requests while payments-api-01 and payments-api-02 were being throttled on CPU.
title: Edge 504s while payments-api pods were throttled on CPU

# orders-db-01: journal growth on /var (sev4)

Tuesday 4 February 2025, 03:05 to 05:05 UTC, 120 minutes. Runbook RB-008. At 03:05 I saw the 90% `/var` alert for orders-db-01, and the next two readings were higher still. Because `/var` shares the root disk on our VMs, a full `/var` would have meant a full root filesystem for the database host, so I dealt with it then rather than leaving it for the morning. While I worked, orders-db answered queries normally and orders-api showed no errors.

The space had gone into `/var/log/journal`, and `journalctl --disk-usage` agreed. A vacuum to 500M brought `/var` well under the threshold straight away. To keep it there I put `SystemMaxUse=500M` into `/etc/systemd/journald.conf`, restarted journald, and stayed with the graph until 05:05, when it had been level for long enough to close.
resolution: Trimmed the journal with a vacuum to 500M and wrote SystemMaxUse=500M into journald.conf on the host so it stays bounded.
root_cause: orders-db-01 had been built without a journald size limit, so the systemd journal under /var/log/journal grew without bound on the shared root disk.
symptoms: The 90% /var alert for orders-db-01 fired overnight and usage kept climbing; the database itself showed no errors.
title: orders-db-01 /var warning traced to an uncapped journal

# Postmortem: feature-cache growth on fraud-scorer-01, 15 February 2025

Prepared by team-risk for the weekly review. Severity sev2. All times UTC. The incident ran from 08:50 to 10:50, a window of 120 minutes.

## Incident record

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Service at fault | fraud-scorer, pod fraud-scorer-01 |
| Who noticed it | payments-api, scoring with static rules instead of the model |
| Contributing system | redis-features-01, answering slowly |
| Codes seen | `FRD-W118` on the scorer, `PAYAPI-W0310` on payments |
| Runbooks consulted | RB-006 for the cache, RB-005 for the memory shape |

## Effect on payments

From 08:50 until the new pods took traffic, payments-api logged `PAYAPI-W0310`: each time a score did not come back in time, it decided with its static rule set instead of the model. Those rules are deliberately coarse. The fallback alert paged at 09:02, and the on-call opened the incident as sev2.

## Sequence of events

- 08:50 `FRD-W118` appears in fraud-scorer-01's logs; payments-api begins logging `PAYAPI-W0310` within that minute.
- 09:02 Page to the team-risk on-call from the payments fallback alert.
- 09:10 Grafana "Container memory (working set)": fraud-scorer-01 had been rising steadily since about 08:50. Pod status showed no restarts.
- 09:18 The on-call worked through RB-005's question of leak versus undersized limit. The previous day's graph was level, traffic this morning was ordinary, and the climb had no peak behind it. A steady rise with flat load points at growth inside the process, so the limit was not touched.
- 09:30 RB-006: `redis-cli --latency` against redis-features-01 returned figures far above its normal range.
- 09:45 The debug build's tracemalloc endpoint on one worker: the fastest-growing allocation site was in the feature cache.
- 10:05 Latency samples from redis-features-01 eased back to normal. `FRD-W118` stopped. Memory did not fall.
- 10:20 Rolling restart of the fraud-scorer Deployment.
- 10:40 New pods serving; working set at its usual baseline; no `PAYAPI-W0310` since the new pods took traffic.
- 10:50 Declared resolved after a quiet watch.

## Analysis

Two things had to be true at once. First, redis-features had to be slow. It is a single node with no failover, and RB-006 lists big key scans and BGSAVE as what usually slows it. This postmortem does not settle which of those, if either, was behind this morning's latency; that sits with the open actions. Second, the scorer had to keep holding what it fetched. The scorer's local feature cache is known to swell whenever the feature store lags, and it did in the fraud-scorer-01 worker traced at 09:45.

Gunicorn's own safety net did not cover it. Each worker is replaced after roughly 5000 requests (`--max-requests`, plus jitter), which caps how long any one worker lives, but the cache grew faster than workers were being replaced. Memory never reached the 3 GiB limit, so no pod was killed.

The scorer stayed up but slow, and payments-api did what it is built to do with a slow scorer. The visible symptom was therefore on the payments side, and the first twenty minutes went to finding which service was actually unwell.

## What worked, what did not

Worked: the payments fallback; RB-005's shape question, which kept us from raising the memory limit and hiding the growth; RB-006's latency check, which tied the growth to a slow store within minutes.

Did not work: nothing alerted on the scorer's own warning rate, and the cache gave nothing back after the store recovered, so a restart was still needed.

## Agreed actions (proposals, no owners assigned)

1. Alert on how often each pod logs `FRD-W118`, not only on the payments fallback.
2. Investigate why the feature cache does not shrink once fetches are fast again.
3. Find out what slowed redis-features this morning.
resolution: Once redis-features latency eased back to normal, fraud-scorer was given a rolling restart; memory returned to its usual level and stayed flat.
root_cause: redis-features-01 was slow and feature fetches ran past their latency budget; while the store was slow, fraud-scorer's in-process feature cache kept growing faster than gunicorn's request-count recycling could reclaim it.
symptoms: payments-api fell back to its static fraud rules (PAYAPI-W0310) for two hours while fraud-scorer-01 logged FRD-W118 and its memory rose in a straight line toward the 3 GiB limit.
title: fraud-scorer-01 memory climb during a slow redis-features morning

# Lookups timing out across three namespaces, evening of 20 February 2025

Platform on-call clock log. sev2, 19:50 to 20:15 UTC. Runbooks opened: RB-020 first, then RB-022.

```
19:50  catalog-api, orders-api, auth-service: name resolution begins failing, all at once
19:56  paged on orders-api checkout errors. Pods print getaddrinfo EAI_AGAIN: the resolver gave
       up waiting; no connection was ever refused
19:58  auth-service-01 and -02 report Go lookup timeouts; catalog-api-01 and catalog-api-02
       report Python resolver errors. Three runtimes, three namespaces, one start
20:00  RB-020 first, since what fails are prod.internal hostnames. dig from a VM at both
       authoritative servers: fast replies, matching SOA serials, records present. internal-dns
       is fine, so we leave those VMs untouched
20:02  so the authoritative side is not it. Failures in three namespaces at once point at the one
       path all three apps share: CoreDNS running as pods inside Kubernetes
20:03  kubectl top for those pods: 2 replicas, each flat against its CPU ceiling
20:05  CoreDNS dashboard: request p99 is measured in seconds now, while the query volume is only
       at the upper end of a normal evening. Pod logs show no errors talking upstream
20:06  decided against a restart: bouncing the pods would cut serving capacity further
20:08  scaled coredns to 4 replicas
20:09  both new pods Ready and answering
20:11  EAI_AGAIN on orders-api-01, orders-api-02 and orders-api-03 dropping away; pooled
       connections had kept working throughout, and fresh ones resolve again
20:15  lookups clean everywhere; closed
```

## Why 2 replicas stopped being enough

No pod asks internal-dns anything. A pod's resolver is cluster CoreDNS, which handles Kubernetes
names itself and relays `prod.internal` questions to internal-dns. Starve those CoreDNS pods of
CPU and every namespace loses name resolution together, while VMs, which query internal-dns
without going through Kubernetes, carry on unbothered. That is what 20:00 and 20:02 showed.

Nobody autoscales coredns; someone picks its size by hand. It was still at 2. Going to 4 roughly
halves what each pod must answer; within minutes of the new pods being Ready, the errors were
fading and lookups came back clean.

## Still to do

- Commit `replicas: 4` to wherever the coredns manifest is kept, so a future redeploy can't put
  it back to 2.
- Note tonight's highest query volume beside the size we chose, and revisit both as the
  cluster grows.
- Alert on CoreDNS request p99 directly. Tonight orders-api told us first.
resolution: coredns went from 2 to 4 replicas at 20:08 and lookups were clean again by 20:15.
root_cause: The kube-system CoreDNS Deployment had 2 replicas, both stuck at their CPU ceiling under evening query load; internal-dns answered normally when asked from a VM.
symptoms: From 19:50 name lookups timed out together in catalog-api, orders-api, auth-service; orders-api logged getaddrinfo EAI_AGAIN whenever it opened a new connection.
title: Cluster DNS ran out of CPU at the evening peak

# Slow processor replies, Saturday 15 March 2025

I took the page for this one, a sev3 that ran from 18:15 to 18:35 UTC, which is 20 minutes. It is a short story, because the cause lay at the processor and little else is known about it.

**How it showed up.** The first signal was the error at the top of the stack: callers of payments-api were being handed `504` on card payments. A gateway timeout says something waited too long, so I looked along the path for the slow hop. payments-api was waiting on card-processor-proxy, and the proxy was waiting on the processor.

**Where the delay was.** Call times to the processor were long on the first egress host and on the second, and both began in the same window. When two separate instances show the same delay together, the delay is unlikely to belong to either of them, and it pointed at the far side of the proxy.

**What the callers got.** A card payment sent to payments-api in those 20 minutes could come back as a gateway timeout instead of an approval or a decline. The payment path is short: payments-api, one of the two proxies, then the processor. The slow step in it was the last one, so the callers above it waited behind that step, and payments-api reported the wait as a timeout.

**What is not known.** Why the processor slowed down is not known. We hold no explanation from the processor, and the request rate toward it during the window was not recorded, so whether our own traffic played a part cannot be said.

**Decisions.** Nothing on our side looked worth restarting or scaling: restarting the proxies would not make the processor reply faster, and neither would more capacity. I watched the call durations and kept the channel informed.

**Outcome.** By 18:35 calls were returning at their usual speed and the `504` responses had stopped.

**Afterwards.** No runbook covers a slow processor. A per-minute record of call duration at the proxy would let the start and end of a spell like this be read from a chart.
resolution: Handled by the payments on-call; the 504 responses had stopped by 18:35.
root_cause: Latency at the external card processor, seen from both proxy hosts.
symptoms: Between 18:15 and 18:35 calls from card-processor-proxy-01 and card-processor-proxy-02 to the card processor took far longer than usual, and callers of payments-api received 504.
title: Card processor latency produced 504 on payment calls

# Tuesday afternoon, fraud-scorer-01, and a CPU graph that lied

I was the team-risk on-call on Tuesday 18 March 2025. This sev3 lasted from 15:10 to 16:05 UTC, and this is how it went from my side.

The first thing I saw was not ours. At 15:14 the payments channel flagged a jump in `PAYAPI-W0310` on payments-api-03.prod.internal: about 40 a second, each one a payment where the fraud score arrived too late and payments-api went ahead with its static rules. Those payments were still decided, by the static rules, but the model was being skipped for a lot of traffic, and that is our problem to fix.

So I opened fraud-scorer. Latency on fraud-scorer-01 had a long, ugly tail. Its CPU, on the other hand, looked relaxed: about 45% of its limit on average over the last quarter hour. My honest first thought was that something downstream of us was slow. I looked at the feature store and found nothing interesting there.

What turned me around was RB-002. A pod that is half idle and still slow is the exact pattern it opens with, so at 15:25 I switched the Grafana "Container CPU" panel to its throttling view. fraud-scorer-01 was at 30% of periods throttled. That is above the roughly 25% that we treat as significant. To be sure the panel was not misleading me, I read `cpu.stat` inside the container twice, a few seconds apart, and `nr_throttled` was climbing right along with `nr_periods`.

The average and the throttling are both true at the same time. The quota is handed out per 100 ms period. When requests arrive in clumps, the pod spends its whole allowance in the first part of a busy period and then waits, frozen, for the next one; quiet periods pull the average back down. Requests that land in a frozen stretch simply wait, and the payments side sees a score that is late.

Why was it spending the allowance so fast? `pgrep -P 1` in the pod listed 16 worker processes. `WEB_CONCURRENCY` was unset in the Deployment, so the entrypoint had counted the cores it could see, all 16 of the node, and started a worker for each. The pod's CPU limit is smaller than 16 cores, so on a busy burst those workers drain the quota in a fraction of the period.

I had two levers: change the worker count, or give the pod more CPU. Changing how gunicorn is started felt like a code change to make in daylight with the team, not in the middle of an incident. So at 15:40 I raised the CPU limit on the fraud-scorer Deployment and left the CPU request where it was, so the scheduler's picture of the pods did not move. The rollout finished at 15:51.

By 15:55 the throttling view on fraud-scorer-01 was below the 25% line and the `PAYAPI-W0310` lines from payments-api-03 had stopped. I watched it until 16:05 and closed it.

Things I want us to talk about this week:

- Matching the worker count to the limit, instead of letting it follow whatever node the pod lands on.
- A throttling alert on fraud-scorer, since the average CPU graph alone hid this one.
- Whether the new limit is the right long-term size or just the quickest fix.
resolution: The CPU limit on the fraud-scorer Deployment was raised with requests left as they were; throttling fell below the 25% line and the fallbacks stopped.
root_cause: fraud-scorer-01 ran one gunicorn worker per visible core of its node, more than its CPU limit could feed; bursts used up the CFS quota early in each period, and 30% of periods were throttled.
symptoms: payments-api-03 logged PAYAPI-W0310 at about 40 per second as fraud scores came back late, while fraud-scorer-01's CPU graph averaged only 45%.
title: A half-busy fraud-scorer-01 that was frozen a third of the time

# The 19 March 2025 zone push, question by question

sev2 · 15:15 to 15:50 UTC · cause internal-dns, seen in orders-api · runbooks: RB-020, RB-027

**What did we see?**

From 15:15 orders-api-02 could not always open new database connections. Each failure was a
lookup of the database hostname answered with NXDOMAIN: as far as that answer went, the name did
not exist. Some lookups still succeeded, so the errors came and went rather than holding steady.
Requests on connections opened before 15:15 kept working.

**What changed at 15:15?**

A change to the `prod.internal` zone file went out through the rollout tool, in a run scoped to
internal-dns-01 alone. It placed the new file there at 15:15 and restarted coredns. The new file
lacked the record orders-api uses for its database. The run touched no other host.

**Why intermittent?**

Pods don't ask internal-dns directly. The cluster CoreDNS sends each `prod.internal` query to one
of the two servers at random and keeps the reply for up to 30 seconds. Only internal-dns-01 served
the new file, so a cache period that happened to land there came back NXDOMAIN and one that went
to the other server came back with the address. orders-api-02 kept drawing both.

**Did the rollout tool notice anything?**

No. It finished with 0 failed hosts. Its only check was the exit status of
`systemctl restart coredns`, and that was 0. CoreDNS came up on internal-dns-01, loaded the zone
and served it. The zone just had one name fewer.

**Was this the "daemon that doesn't come back" case?**

We opened RB-027 because a config push started it. The danger RB-027 warns about is a process
that dies after systemd has already called the restart a success; its example is the `kafka`
unit, which is `Type=simple`, so systemd reports success the moment its process is spawned.
That did not fit. `systemctl is-active coredns` on internal-dns-01 returned active and it answered
an SOA query. The daemon was fine; the file it served was not.

**How did we pin it down?**

Paged at 15:26 on orders-api's connection errors. At 15:31, from a VM, we asked each server for
the name directly and compared SOA serials, as RB-020 lays out. internal-dns-01 had a newer serial
and answered NXDOMAIN; the server the run had not touched still had the older serial and returned
the record. A record that one copy of the zone has and the newer copy lacks points at the change
itself, and the diff of the 15:15 push showed the record removed.

**How was it fixed?**

The record went back into the zone source with a higher serial, and the corrected file went out
through the same tool to internal-dns-01 at 15:38, again with 0 failed hosts. Once the cluster
cache turned over, lookups from orders-api-02 resolved every time; the last failed one was logged
at 15:38. We watched until 15:50 and closed: 35 minutes from the first push.

**What should change?**

- Before a zone push: list the records the new file removes compared with the live one, and stop
  for a person to confirm each removal.
- After the push: ask the server for a handful of names that must always exist, rather than
  trusting the restart's exit code.
- An NXDOMAIN rate for `prod.internal` names seen by pods, so the page names DNS and not the
  database connection.
resolution: The record was restored with a higher SOA serial and the corrected file pushed to internal-dns-01 at 15:38; the lookups recovered as the cluster DNS cache turned over.
root_cause: A prod.internal zone-file change pushed by the rollout tool to internal-dns-01 no longer contained the record orders-api connects to; coredns restarted cleanly there, so the run reported 0 failed hosts.
symptoms: From 15:15 orders-api-02 intermittently failed new database connections because the lookup of its database hostname came back NXDOMAIN.
title: Zone push dropped a name orders-api needed

# Slow payments traced to payments-pgbouncer-01

sev3 · 2025-03-22 · 14:15 to 15:00 UTC · cause: high_cpu · affected: payments-api · runbooks: RB-011, RB-002

| Where | UTC | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| payments-api | 14:15 | Latency on the payment routes began to rise. Requests that could not get a pooled connection within 500 ms logged `PAYAPI-E1042` and returned an error. |
| on-call | during the incident | Treated it as a latency complaint first, so RB-002 was on the table alongside RB-011. |
| payments-pgbouncer-01 | during the incident | Showed clients waiting at the same time as server connections that were not in use. That combination, plus the CPU reading on the VM, pointed at the PgBouncer process itself. |
| payments-pgbouncer-01 | during the incident | `top` showed the PgBouncer process at 100% of one core. The bouncer runs as a single process using one core, so that core was the ceiling for everything it served. |
| team-payments infra | during the incident | The problem was escalated to them. |
| payments-api | 15:00 | Connections acquired within the deadline again and `PAYAPI-E1042` was gone. Closed. |

## Scale of the exposure

payments-api runs 4 pods with a pool of 40 connections each, 160 client connections in all, and each payments-pgbouncer instance normally carries about half of them. When the one doing the work on payments-pgbouncer-01 stalls, the pods that route through it wait, hold their pooled connections, and hit the 500 ms acquire deadline. That is the path from a busy proxy to the application's error code.

## Decisions

- Pool sizes were left unchanged. Nothing in the evidence called for them, and changing a pool does not help a process that is out of CPU.
- The bouncer was escalated. What team-payments infra did next is not recorded here, only that by 15:00 the errors had stopped.

## Follow-ups

- Alert on CPU of the PgBouncer process directly, so a pinned core is visible before the application's error code appears.
- Add a line to RB-002's checklist for the case where latency has no throttling behind it and the slow component is a single-threaded proxy.
resolution: The bouncer problem was escalated to team-payments infra; by 15:00 payments-api acquired connections within its deadline again and PAYAPI-E1042 had stopped.
root_cause: PgBouncer on payments-pgbouncer-01 is a single process using one core, and that core was saturated while its server connections were still idle, so the bouncer was the bottleneck rather than the pool or the database.
symptoms: From 14:15 payments-api latency rose and it logged PAYAPI-E1042 when a pool connection could not be acquired in time.
title: Payment calls slowed behind a PgBouncer process at one core

sev2, 09:00 to 09:53 UTC. auth-service against auth-db. Condensed by role, oldest first. Runbook

**09:38 identity on-call:** paged on the login error rate. `/v1/auth/login` is returning `503`,

**09:40 identity on-call:** each auth-service pod (auth-service-01, auth-service-02) logs failed
dials to auth-db-01 with `x509: certificate has expired` in the error. Only fresh connections
fail. Pooled ones from before the expiry still work, which is why some logins get through.

**09:42 dba on-call:** auth-db-01 looks healthy from the inside. Nothing in its log, fewer client
connections than usual. That fits clients that never finish the handshake.

**09:44 dba on-call:** working from RB-024. The certificate file on disk is a renewed one, put
there by the renewal timer on 2025-03-09, and its expiry is well ahead.

**09:47 dba on-call:** `s_client` against auth-db-01: what the server hands out carries a
different serial from that file, and that certificate ran out at 09:00 today. Postgres has kept
the previous certificate in memory, and nothing has reloaded it since the files changed.

**09:49 identity lead:** that explains the slow climb. Our pool retires a connection after an
hour, or after half an hour idle, both set in the `DATABASE_URL`. Every connection retired since
expiry can't be replaced.

**09:50 identity lead:** for the record, we are not switching auth-service to `sslmode=require`
to buy time. It would stop checking whose certificate it is talking to. It stays `verify-full`.

**09:51 dba on-call:** `SELECT pg_reload_conf();` on auth-db-01. `s_client` now shows the renewed
serial. A reload, not a restart, so open sessions are left alone.

**09:52 dba on-call:** `pg_reload_conf()` on auth-db-02, the replica, as
well. Done.

**09:53 identity on-call:** new connections succeed, the `503`s have stopped, logins look normal.
Closing.

- Make the renewal job reload Postgres as its last step.
- Alert on the expiry of whatever certificate each server actually presents, not on the file.
  The file had been fine for the whole month leading up to this; 2025-03-09 to today is 30 days.
- After any certificate change on auth-db, compare presented serial against the file, on both
  hosts.

# ledger-service-02 OOMKilled on 21 April 2025: questions and answers

ledger squad, sev3, 18:05 to 22:30 UTC. We worked from RB-005 and RB-001.

**What happened?**

ledger-service-02 was restarted by Kubernetes, and the pod's last state read `OOMKilled` (exit code 137). The container had passed its memory limit and the kernel ended the process without warning. The incident ran from 18:05 to 22:30.

**Was it the limit or the service?**

The working-set panel showed memory climbing steadily on ledger-service-02 before the kill, which is the pattern RB-005 associates with a leak. A limit that was merely too small would have shown flat memory until a peak. We therefore did not treat a larger limit as the answer.

**Why is a JVM involved at all?**

ledger-service is a Java 17 process, PID 1 in its container, with its heap set by `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75`. A heap that keeps expanding walks the whole container towards its limit. The collector's log is `/var/log/ledger/gc.log`, and that is where the history of collections can be read.

**How did it end?**

The replacement pod came up and ran normally; we closed at 22:30. A leak ticket was opened, and its heap summary was taken from the new process as its memory grew again, because the first one's heap went when it was killed.

**Which two documents did we use, and for what?**

RB-005 is the team-platform FAQ on killed pods. It supplied the question we asked first: does memory rise steadily or sit flat until a peak? RB-001 is the ledger-service runbook for the JVM, and it supplied the garbage-collection and heap context for what a growing heap looks like.

**What did the kill do to the evidence?**

A killed process takes its heap with it, so anything we learned about what had grown had to come from the restarted process after it climbed again. That limits how much the ticket can say about the original run.

**What is the ticket still expected to answer?**

The ticket owns the question of what grew. No object type, code path or heap-dump finding has been identified so far.

**What changes?**

- Follow the leak ticket to find the source of the growth.
- Revisit the memory limit only if kills return.
resolution: A leak ticket was opened with a heap summary from the replacement process as it grew again; the memory limit was not raised.
root_cause: The JVM heap on ledger-service-02 kept growing until the container exceeded its memory limit and the kernel killed it; the growth looked like a leak rather than a limit that was too small.
symptoms: ledger-service-02 was restarted with reason OOMKilled; its memory graph had been rising steadily before the kill.
title: ledger-service-02 killed for memory after a steady heap climb

**The deadline.** payments-api waits at most half a second (`DB_ACQUIRE_TIMEOUT=500ms`) for a pooled connection. Past that it logs `PAYAPI-E1042` and answers `503`. On a healthy day the 99th-percentile wait is under 50 ms, so every error here was a request that waited ten times longer than normal and still got nothing.

**Why the database.** A connection returns to the pool when its query finishes, so long-running queries on payments-db-01 keep connections out. With the pools at their 40-connection ceiling on payments-api-03 and payments-api-04, new requests had nowhere to go.

**Share of capacity.** Four pods at 40 connections each make 4 x 40 = 160 client-side connections. The two full pools, 2 x 40 = 80, were half of that.

**Runbook.** RB-010 covers pgx pool exhaustion. Neither the query behind this one nor the reason it was slow is known, and nothing explains why only these two pods filled.
resolution: team-payments took the incident; PAYAPI-E1042 and the 503 responses stopped by 02:20.
root_cause: Slow queries on payments-db-01 kept the pgx pools on payments-api-03 and payments-api-04 checked out, so new requests could not get a connection before the DB_ACQUIRE_TIMEOUT deadline.
symptoms: payments-api-03 and payments-api-04 returned 503 on payment routes and logged PAYAPI-E1042 as requests ran into the 500ms wait for a database connection.

# Ticket: ledger-service-01 loses its database address now and then

**Service:** ledger-service (pod ledger-service-01.prod.internal) · **Sev:** sev3 · **Date:** 2025-05-02
**Window:** 06:30 to 07:45 UTC · **Also involved:** internal-dns-01.prod.internal · **Refs:** RB-020, RB-027

## What was observed

From 06:30 ledger-service-01 logged refusals when it tried to take a fresh database connection. Every error is about a name that could not be turned into an address, and the DNS status in it is `NXDOMAIN`. Between the refusals the same pod managed to connect. The pattern held for 75 minutes, 06:30 to 07:45, with this pod the only one named.

## Effect on the service

Anything in ledger-service-01 that needed a new database connection while a bad answer was cached had to fail, because the name of the database was reported as non-existent for that stretch. The next refresh of the resolver cache could go the other way, which is why the service seemed to recover and relapse without any change on the pod. The ledger database is not suspected: the error is raised before any connection to it is attempted.

## Thread

**ledger on-call:** the message is about the name of the ledger database, not about waiting for a free connection, so this is not a ledger problem. Passing it to platform.

**platform on-call:** a zone-file push to internal-dns-01 went out just before 06:30, and the tool summarised it as 0 failed hosts. `prod.internal` lookups from a pod pass through the cluster resolver, which hands each one to either internal-dns machine and remembers the answer for up to 30 s. With two machines holding different zones, answers arrive alternately right and wrong.

**platform on-call:** A push was involved, so RB-027 got a look. It covers units that look started and then fail, and uses `kafka` (stated as `Type=simple`) for illustration. `coredns` showed no sign of having stopped, so the useful question became the contents of internal-dns-01's zone file. That belongs to RB-020, which suggests querying both servers for the same name and putting their serials side by side.

**platform on-call:** the file on internal-dns-01 lacked the ledger database record. Quiet from 07:45, and the ticket was closed at that point with the work handed to the platform team.

## Why the zone and not the pod

Two facts point away from ledger-service-01 itself. The message names a failed lookup, which happens before the database is contacted, and the failures began at the minute a zone-file push reached internal-dns-01. An application fault would not line up with a DNS push, and a database fault would not produce a DNS status in the error text.

## Handoff

Ownership: team-platform. Why the record was absent from the pushed file, and what brought the errors to an end, were not recorded. RB-020 carries a remedy for this class of fault; whether it was used is unknown. Failed attempts were not counted, so the size of the impact is unknown.

Idea for later: when a zone push reaches only one internal-dns machine, look at the other one's answer for a service-critical name before the run is called finished.
resolution: team-platform took the ticket; the lookups stopped failing by 07:45.
root_cause: A zone-file push left internal-dns-01 serving a prod.internal file without the ledger database record, so the cluster resolver received NXDOMAIN whenever it forwarded to that server; the rollout run reported 0 failed hosts.
symptoms: From 06:30 ledger-service-01 intermittently failed to reach its database because lookups of the ledger database record were answered NXDOMAIN.
title: ledger-service-01 failing to resolve its database after a zone push to internal-dns-01

# 4 May 2025: auth-service-01 and the goroutines that stayed

sev3 · 12:35 to 21:25 UTC · runbook: RB-005 · host: auth-service-01

```
12:35  start: auth-service-01 is OOMKilled while its goroutine count climbs
21:25  end: the kills have stopped
```

Between those two lines no other clock time was written down.

## Summary of the day

For 530 minutes, from 12:35 to 21:25, one authentication pod, auth-service-01, was killed by the kernel for going past its container memory limit. Kubernetes marked each kill `OOMKilled`. This was a memory leak, and it showed in two graphs that rose together: the pod's memory, and the count of goroutines inside the process. RB-005 is the runbook for killed pods and was the one that applied.

## What a rising goroutine count says

Goroutines are the unit of concurrent work in a Go service. Each one holds a stack and everything it references, and a goroutine that never returns keeps both alive. A count that only rises therefore means work is being started and never finishing, and memory grows in step with it until the container limit cuts the process off. That points at unfinished work and away from one oversized buffer, but it stops short of a cause: naming the code that started the goroutines needs a goroutine profile, and none was kept.

## Where the evidence ends

- No goroutine profile exists, so no code path is described here.
- No count of kills was written down.
- Only auth-service-01 is named; nothing is recorded about the service's other pod.
- What ended the kills is not in the record.

## Ownership and close

The on-call took the incident, and by 21:25 the kills had stopped.

## What to do differently

Capture a goroutine profile from the pod early in a climb, while its count is still high but the container has not yet been killed. After the next restart that evidence is gone.
resolution: The on-call took the incident at sev3; the kills stopped by 21:25.
root_cause: Goroutines accumulated in auth-service-01 until the container reached its memory limit and was killed; which code path started them was not recorded.
symptoms: auth-service-01 was OOMKilled between 12:35 and 21:25 as its memory climbed with its goroutine count.

A full pool on catalog-api usually sends people straight to the database's connection limit, which is what RB-012 covers. So the first check on catalog-db-01 was the session count: 32 sessions against 97 usable slots, CPU low. That is far from the ceiling, which ruled the limit out and moved attention to what the sessions were waiting on.

Roughly 60 misses and 5 writes reach the database each second, about 65 requests a second. A stalled request keeps its pooled connection, and the pods hold only 30 between them, so the pool drained almost immediately. catalog-api-01 and catalog-api-02 began logging QueuePool timeouts at 14:02:30, which fits requests that had started waiting for a connection thirty seconds earlier.

14:02     release migration on products starts and stalls
14:02:15  first 504 at the edge
14:02:30  QueuePool timeouts begin on catalog-api-01 and catalog-api-02

14:09     migration cancelled; 504s stop within the minute

# Postmortem: the edge's certificate file, 15 May 2025

Thursday 15 May 2025, 16:07 to 16:32 UTC, 25 minutes, sev1. Team: team-platform. Runbook: RB-025.

## Impact

For 25 minutes some of the people and programs that talk to our public edge could not open a TLS connection. The edge is three pods, edge-gateway-03, edge-gateway-01 and edge-gateway-02, and all three were serving the same incomplete certificate file. Which clients failed depended on what they already held: those without a stored copy of the intermediate could not finish the handshake, and the rest carried on. For a refused client the failure came before any HTTP was sent, so the routes behind the edge never saw its requests. That makes the damage uneven by nature, and no measure of its size was kept: neither the number of refused connections nor the share of callers.

Browsers, mobile apps and partner integrations are the clients that validate the certificate, so any of them could be among the refused.

## How it was found

The check that separated this from other certificate faults was a handshake attempt with `openssl s_client` against the pods. It ended in verify code 21, the code RB-025 attaches to an intermediate missing from the served file. A lapsed leaf gives a different code, and a wrong device clock would have shown up as one caller failing, not as trouble across the edge. Code 21 on the pods put the fault in the file the pods serve.

## What the file was

The certificate comes from a public CA and is stored in the Secret `edge-public-tls`, from which each pod mounts it as files. On this day those files held the certificate for our own name and no intermediate beside it. Since all three pods read the same files, the choice of pod could not help a client. Envoy reads the certificate when a pod starts, so a changed Secret reaches a pod only through a restart of the Deployment; team-platform renews the certificate 30 days ahead of expiry.

## Ending

The record holds two clock times, the start at 16:07 and the end at 16:32, and everything in between is undated. team-platform took the incident, and by 16:32 handshakes were succeeding again. The change that ended it was not recorded. RB-025 gives the remedy for a missing intermediate as a single file with our certificate first and the intermediate after it. How the intermediate came to be missing is not recorded.

## Proposals

1. Keep the per-minute handshake and request counts from the listener stats alongside every change to the Secret, so a before and after can be compared directly.
2. Whenever the Secret's files change, list the certificates the new file contains and keep that list with the change.
resolution: team-platform took the incident; handshakes were succeeding again by 16:32.
root_cause: The certificate file served by all three edge pods held the certificate for our own name but not the intermediate above it, so clients that did not already have the intermediate could not build a chain to the public CA; how the intermediate came to be missing is not recorded.
symptoms: From 16:07 clients without a cached copy of the intermediate failed their TLS handshakes with all three edge pods (edge-gateway-01, edge-gateway-02, edge-gateway-03), and an openssl check returned verify code 21.
title: Edge pods presented a certificate file with no intermediate

# Evening handoff, 22 May 2025: auth-service logins failing

Rated sev2. The trouble began at 21:32 UTC and was over at 21:52, so it lasted 20 minutes. Hosts: auth-service-01 and auth-service-02. Runbook opened: RB-010.

## Current state

Logins are working again. From 21:32 sign-ins slowed, and 503 responses from auth-service followed for the rest of the 20 minutes; the cause sat one layer down, in auth-db, which was slow to answer. The incident is closed and this note carries the follow-ups.

## What was going on

auth-service talks to its database through a pgx connection pool capped at 30 connections per pod. With two pods that is 2 x 30 = 60 connections in total. auth-service's own 60 fits inside auth-db's 200. The shortage was inside the service. Each login needs a connection, and while auth-db was slow every connection stayed checked out far longer than usual. New logins found the pool empty and waited behind the ones in progress.

The `503` is auth-service's own doing. The service has a ceiling: once more than 64 logins per pod are in flight at the same time, it returns `503` straight away. The first `503`s appeared when the waiting logins reached that ceiling, a few minutes after the slowdown began. It is not a message from auth-db and not a timeout from the pool; auth-service has no separate acquire timeout of its own.

## Where RB-010 fits

RB-010 is the reference card for a pgx pool running dry, written around payments-api, and it is the runbook cited for this incident. Its pool-exhaustion reading applies to auth-service; its acquire-deadline details do not, since auth-service has neither.

## What is not known

- Which query was slow was not recorded.
- Why auth-db became slow was not recorded.
- What ended the slowness was not recorded; the `503`s stopped by 21:52.

## Next shift

1. Someone from the database side should say what slowed auth-db at 21:32, if the logs still hold it.
2. Alert on pool occupancy per auth-service pod, so the page arrives before logins start being refused.
3. The 64-per-pod ceiling and the 30-per-pod pool are separate limits. Whoever changes one should look at the other.
resolution: The auth on-call took the incident and the 503s had stopped by 21:52; what ended the slow queries was not recorded.
root_cause: Slow queries on auth-db kept auth-service's pgxpool connections checked out, 30 per pod across 2 pods, so logins queued inside the service until it started refusing them with its own 503.

# Reservations waiting on row locks in inventory-db-01

sev2 · 2025-06-04 · 15:55 to 17:30 UTC · affected: inventory-service, orders-api · runbook: RB-015

| Who or what | UTC | Seen |
|---|---|---|
| inventory-service-01, inventory-service-02 | 15:55 | Stock reservations time out on both instances, each logged as `INV-E220`. |
| orders-api | during the window | Checkout depends on the stock check, so orders-api is where customers feel the delay. It is a symptom service here; the inventory code is the one that identifies the incident. |
| inventory-db-01 | during the window | The sessions showed lock waits on the `reservations` table. The holder is not known. |
| inventory squad | 17:30 | `INV-E220` stopped on both instances. Closed. |

## Impact and cause

RB-015 is the card cited for slow stock reservations; this incident falls in its lock-wait part. A reservation writes to `reservations`, and a write to a row that another transaction holds a lock on cannot proceed until that transaction ends. While the lock lasted, the writes queued behind it, and each one eventually ran past the service's timeout and was logged as `INV-E220`.

The service side explains how widely it spread. inventory-service uses a pool of 20 connections per instance, so the two instances together hold 2 x 20 = 40 connections. While lock waits lasted, those connections could be taken by requests that were waiting, and new reservations queued behind them.

## What this was not

It was not a missing index. Nor was it a shortage of connection slots: the service's 40 connections are well under inventory-db's 97 usable ones (100 minus 3).

## Open points

- Which session held the locks, and what it was doing, was not recorded.
- Whether the locks came from a release, a manual session or a batch was not recorded.
- What released them was not recorded. The inventory squad handled it, and `INV-E220` was gone by 17:30.

## Follow-ups

- Record the blocking session's details as soon as lock waits appear, since they are gone once the lock is released.
- Add a lock-wait panel for inventory-db-01 to the dashboard the squad opens first.

# Questions and answers: the redis-cache failover of 19 June 2025

sev4. 02:25 to 02:40 UTC on 19 June 2025, 15 minutes. Hosts: redis-cache-01 and redis-cache-02. Runbook: RB-017.

**Was anything broken?**

No fault caused this. The primary of redis-cache, the master called `cache`, was handed over from redis-cache-01 to redis-cache-02 by choice. `SENTINEL FAILOVER <master name>` is the documented way to ask for such a move. The record does not say why the move was planned, or who ran it.

**What did customers see?**

catalog-api logged `CAT-E301` for under a minute from 02:25. That code means a product read could not be served from the cache and was answered from catalog-db instead, so those reads took the slower path. How many reads were affected was not recorded.

**Why does a brief CAT-E301 matter?**

RB-017 is written to protect catalog-db when the cache goes away, because a read that misses the cache becomes a query on the database. No database trouble is recorded for this incident.

**What is redis-cache made of?**

It is Redis 7 with one primary and one replica, redis-cache-01 and redis-cache-02, and Sentinel manages which of them is primary. The master name `cache` is how Sentinel refers to the pair. Before the move the primary was redis-cache-01; afterwards it was redis-cache-02.

**Was it an automatic failover?**

No. An automatic failover happens when Sentinel judges the primary unreachable. Here the primary was healthy and the handover was a deliberate act.

**Which hosts took part?**

redis-cache-01 held the primary role until the move and redis-cache-02 held it afterwards. Both appear in the logs around the move.

**What became of redis-cache-01?**

Its state after the handover is not recorded. Three Sentinel processes watch the `cache` master with a quorum of 2, and any of them can answer that question. The current primary can be read from Sentinel with `SENTINEL get-master-addr-by-name cache`, a query given in RB-017.

**When was it over?**

By 02:40 catalog-api was reading from the cache again. The 15 minutes run from the first entry at 02:25 to that point, while the `CAT-E301` lines themselves lasted under a minute.

**Who handled it?**

team-platform took the incident.
resolution: team-platform took the incident; catalog-api was reading from the cache again by 02:40.
root_cause: The primary role for the master named cache was moved on purpose from redis-cache-01 to redis-cache-02; for a short time catalog-api could not get product data from the cache and read from the database. Why the failover was planned is not recorded.
symptoms: During a planned failover of the redis-cache primary from redis-cache-01 to redis-cache-02, catalog-api logged CAT-E301 for a short time while it read product data from the database instead of the cache.
title: Planned failover of redis-cache from redis-cache-01 to redis-cache-02

# Refunds export starved the payments bouncers (sev2)

**When:** 2025-06-24, 13:20 to 14:05 UTC · **Owner:** team-payments · **Runbooks used:** RB-011, RB-010

## Summary

For 45 minutes on a Tuesday afternoon, card payments slowed down and a growing share of them failed with `503`. payments-api logged `PAYAPI-E1042` on all four pods. Nothing had crashed. A refunds export that finance ops had asked for was running inside payments-api itself, and its long transactions occupied the database connections that live payment traffic needed. The queue for those connections formed inside PgBouncer, on both instances at once.

## Impact

- `/v1/payments/*` latency started rising around 13:20. Failures followed within minutes and were worst around 13:40.
- A request that could not get a pool connection inside payments-api's 500 ms acquire deadline returned `503`. Customers saw a failed payment and could try again.
- Postgres itself had connections to spare throughout.

## How it looked at first

The page at 13:24 was on the `503` rate for payment routes. The pool panels told the familiar story from RB-010: 40 of 40 connections acquired on every pod, acquire wait p99 pinned at the deadline. RB-010 then asks what the database sessions are doing. They were `active`, not idle inside an open transaction, so the pods were not sitting on transactions while calling something else. They were waiting in line.

## Investigation

- 13:31 · `SHOW POOLS` on payments-pgbouncer-01 and payments-pgbouncer-02. Both the same: `sv_active` at 50 (40 regular plus 10 reserve), no idle server connections, `cl_waiting` near 30, `maxwait` near 4 s.
- 13:34 · `SHOW CLIENTS` counted about 80 payments-api clients per instance. An even split, so neither bouncer was carrying the other's share.
- 13:36 · the pgbouncer process on payments-pgbouncer-02 was far below a full core. The bouncer was not the bottleneck.
- 13:41 · on payments-db, `pg_stat_activity` grouped by statement: one statement held about 90 sessions with transactions averaging about 2 s. It was the export's.
- 13:44 · about 100 client backends out of 200 allowed by `max_connections`. The database had headroom; the wait lived entirely in the bouncers.

## Why the numbers fit together

Each of the four pods may hold 40 connections (`pool_max_conns=40`), so up to 160 client-side connections, roughly 80 landing on each bouncer. A bouncer opens at most 50 server connections. With all 50 busy, about 80 − 50 = 30 clients are left waiting, which is what `cl_waiting` showed. Two bouncers open at most 2 × 50 = 100 server connections, which matches the backend count.

Waits hovered around 4 s. That is past the 3 s after which the reserve pool opens, and well short of the 10 s after which PgBouncer disconnects a waiting client. So no client was dropped by the bouncer; every failure was payments-api giving up at its own deadline.

A transaction-pooled bouncer lends a server connection to a client for one transaction and takes it back at commit. Payment transactions last milliseconds. The export's took about 2 s each and were issued back to back from all four pods, enough to keep about 90 of the 100 server connections on the two bouncers occupied.

## Root cause

The export started at 13:10. It used the same pgx pool, the same database role and the same transaction-mode bouncers as live payments, and nothing capped how many export transactions could be in flight.

## Resolution

- 13:50 · export switched off.
- 13:51 · remaining export statements cancelled with `pg_cancel_backend`. `cl_waiting` dropped to 0 on both bouncers.
- 13:52 · `PAYAPI-E1042` stopped.
- 14:05 · resolved after 13 quiet minutes.

We followed RB-011 and did not raise `pool_max_conns` or `default_pool_size`: more clients would only have lengthened that queue.

## Follow-ups

1. Run exports outside the payment request path, with their own small pool. Owner: team-payments.
2. Alert when `cl_waiting` stays above 0 on either bouncer for a minute, so the page names the queue instead of the `503`s.
3. Exports that finance needs during the day get a size and concurrency review first.
resolution: The export was turned off and its remaining statements cancelled; the bouncer queues drained within a minute.
root_cause: A refunds export running inside payments-api held server connections for about 2 s per transaction and occupied about 90 of the 100 server connections on payments-pgbouncer-01 and payments-pgbouncer-02.
symptoms: Payment requests slowed, then failed with 503 and PAYAPI-E1042 on every payments-api pod while clients queued inside both PgBouncer instances.
title: Refunds export starved the payments bouncers

# Wednesday 9 July 2025: checkout slowed by a new filter with no index

This was a sev3 for the inventory team, open from 10:40 until 15:30 UTC: 290 minutes.

**The effect.** Checkout was where it hurt. Stock reservations were timing out, so inventory-service-01 and inventory-service-02 both logged `INV-E220`, and orders-api-01, orders-api-02 and orders-api-03 passed the failure up as `ORD-5003`. The database underneath, inventory-db-01, looked busy rather than idle.

**The cause.** That morning's release changed the reservation query so that it filtered on `expires_at`. The column had no index. Postgres therefore answered every reservation by scanning the whole `reservations` table, one row after another, and that was the work keeping inventory-db-01 busy. The inventory pools hold 20 connections per pod, 2 x 20 = 40 in all, and with every query taking longer, those connections stayed occupied and callers queued up to their timeout.

**How we knew.** Two things carried most of the weight. The errors were on both inventory pods at the same moment and the database was working hard, which together pointed at a query and away from one sick pod. After that, the slow statement's plan showed a sequential scan on `reservations` with a filter on `expires_at`, which matched what the release had added. The procedure is in RB-015; I won't repeat it here.

**The fix.** We built the missing index, `reservations_expires_at_idx`, with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, so that reservations and other writes could carry on while it was built. This was chosen over backing out the release. The build and the recovery both fell in the afternoon, and the incident was closed at 15:30.

**Who was affected.** Anyone checking out during the window could hit the failure. The effect travelled in a chain: the database was slow, inventory-service timed out on its reservation, and orders-api reported the failed call on checkout. Each hop logged its own code, which is why the same incident left three different traces in three services.

**Since then.** The table now has the index and the reservation filter runs against it. When a release adds a filter on a column, the question to ask at review is whether an index covers that column in the table the query reads.
resolution: reservations_expires_at_idx was built concurrently in the same afternoon, and reservations were fast again by 15:30.
root_cause: A release added a filter on reservations.expires_at, a column with no index, so inventory-db-01 ran sequential scans on reservations for each reservation query.
symptoms: Stock reservations timed out with INV-E220 on both inventory-service pods, and orders-api logged ORD-5003 on checkout.

# Wednesday 16 July 2025: 504s that traced back to a node

sev3 · 05:50 to 06:35 UTC · cause on the edge's node · runbook: RB-014

**What went wrong, from the outside?**

From 05:50 requests passing through edge-gateway-03 came back as `504`. More than one route was affected, so this was not a single endpoint misbehaving. The window ran 45 minutes, to 06:35.

Because the errors were not tied to one route. When a single service is slow, its route shows the `504`s and its owners get the call. Here the common element was the gateway pod that carried the requests, so the useful question was what that pod shared with everything it served.

The incident opened at 05:50 and was closed at 06:35, 45 minutes later. The record does not hold a mid-incident change on the pods, the routes or the upstream services; the shape is a start, a hand-off to the owning team, and an end.

team-platform, as the runbook directs for shared causes. The 504s had stopped by 06:35.

The evidence we have places the problem on the node under edge-gateway-03, and the pod was the place where it showed up. We did not record a node-level message or a metric that proves how the pressure arose, and we are not claiming one.

**Why was a restart of the pod not the answer we recorded?**

Nothing here says a restart was tried or helped. The runbook's shared-cause entry points to the node pool and its owner, so that is where the ticket went.

**Open items**

- Record, next time, which signal on the node first showed the pressure, so the pod does not have to be the thing we reason from.
- Keep `504` on several routes at once as the cue to look below the services.

# RISK ticket: fraud-scorer-02 memory keeps rising

**Opened:** 22 July 2025, 08:15 UTC, by the team-risk on-call
**Severity:** sev3
**Component:** fraud-scorer
**Hosts in scope:** fraud-scorer-02.prod.internal, redis-features-01.prod.internal
**Reference:** RB-006
**State:** Resolved 11:00 UTC

## Description

The routine memory review this morning put fraud-scorer-02 at the top of `kubectl top pod` for the scorer, well above its sibling and higher each time the command was repeated. No restarts, no kills so far. Raising a ticket rather than paging, since nothing customer-facing is broken yet. A few `PAYAPI-W0310` lines have shown up on the payments side.

## Comments

**08:31, on-call.** The odd part is the gap between the two pods, so starting there. Counted `FRD-W118` per pod over the last stretch of logs: fraud-scorer-02 has several times as many as its sibling. Both pods read from the same feature store, so whatever is slow is hitting -02 harder.

**08:44, on-call.** `py-spy dump` on two workers of fraud-scorer-02 (the debug image has `SYS_PTRACE`). Most threads sit in the feature client waiting for a reply. They are not busy; they are queued.

**09:02, on-call.** `redis-cli --latency` against redis-features-01: mostly low samples, broken up by regular spikes far above normal. That is the slow read the warnings complain about.

**09:20, on-call.** Lined up the memory panel against the `FRD-W118` counts for fraud-scorer-02. Every bump in warnings is followed by a step up in working set, and the steps never come back down. The sibling, with far fewer warnings, has barely moved. RB-006's known pattern, seen from the outside.

**09:41, team-risk lead.** Holding the restart for now. While the store is still spiking, new pods would just start filling up again. Let's see if the spikes settle.

**10:05, on-call.** Per RB-006, a slow feature store usually means a heavy key scan or a BGSAVE on it. It is a single node with no replica to take reads, so anything heavy on it reaches every feature fetch. Asked team-platform to look at the store's side.

**10:20, on-call.** Latency samples on redis-features-01 back at their usual floor. `FRD-W118` on fraud-scorer-02 is down to zero.

**10:24, on-call.** Working set on fraud-scorer-02 is flat but not falling. Gunicorn replaces a worker after `--max-requests 5000` (with `--max-requests-jitter 500`), so memory would come back only as workers cycle out. Taking the RB-006 restart instead of waiting on that.

**10:30, on-call.** `rollout restart` on the fraud-scorer Deployment issued.

**10:44, on-call.** New pods up. fraud-scorer-02 now level with its sibling. No new `PAYAPI-W0310` since the restart finished.

**11:00, on-call.** Quiet. Resolving.

## Closing notes

- The memory review caught this before anything paged. Comparing the two pods side by side was the quickest lead.
- Holding the restart until the store settled meant one restart was enough.
- fraud-scorer-02 took many more slow reads than its sibling, and its memory tracked those warnings step for step. Why one pod was hit harder is open.

## Open questions

1. Why did fraud-scorer-02 see so many more slow reads than the other pod from the same store?
2. Should the memory review flag a gap between the two scorer pods, not only an absolute level?
3. Is a 5000-request recycle short enough for a cache that grows in steps like this?
resolution: redis-features latency eased at 10:20 and fraud-scorer was restarted at 10:30; memory settled at its normal level and the warnings ended.
root_cause: redis-features-01 answered slowly; while reads were slow, the scorer's in-process feature cache on fraud-scorer-02 grew without giving memory back.
symptoms: fraud-scorer-02 topped the pod memory list and kept growing; it logged FRD-W118 far more than its sibling, and payments-api logged PAYAPI-W0310 for scores that came back late.
title: Ticket: fraud-scorer-02 resident memory creeping while feature reads lagged

# The Sunday login flood

I was on call for team-identity on Sunday 3 August 2025. This is my account of a sev2 that ran from 10:10 to 10:45 UTC.

The page came at 10:14: the edge's `503` rate on `/v1/auth/login` was over its threshold. Other routes looked fine at first glance. The login graph didn't: attempts had gone from the usual 15 or so a second to about 150 a second at 10:08, and about 97% of them were failing on the password. They came from a wide spread of addresses. That pattern is credential stuffing, someone replaying leaked username and password pairs against us.

auth-service checks each password with bcrypt on the request goroutine. bcrypt is meant to be expensive, which is the point when someone steals the hashes and the problem when someone floods the login form. Each pod also caps itself: once 64 logins are in flight it answers `503` instead of queueing more, and the edge passed those straight through. The first ones went out at 10:10.

At 10:20 I worked through RB-002, because both pods were sitting exactly at their CPU limit. The throttling view showed about 70% of periods throttled, which on its own would send you looking for a thread count sized to the node. That wasn't it. Our Deployment sets `GOMAXPROCS` from the CPU limit, and it was 2 on both auth-service-01 and auth-service-02, matching the limit. This wasn't a mismatch making a half-idle pod stall; the pods really needed more CPU than the 2 they were allowed.

There is no rate limit on the login route at the edge; the only edge limit we have is on `/search`. So the quickest lever was the one RB-002 describes. At 10:27 I raised the CPU limit from 2 to 4 per pod and left the requests alone, so scheduling didn't change. The Deployment rolled one extra pod at a time with none taken away, and was done at 10:33. The `503`s stopped at 10:34, while the attempts were still arriving at the same rate. At 10:40 the attempts stopped as abruptly as they had started. I watched for five more minutes and closed it at 10:45.

What I'd like done:

1. A rate limit on `/v1/auth/login`, per client address and overall. It's not built, and nothing at the edge could have helped today.
2. An alert on the share of failed logins, which would have fired before the CPU did.
3. Keep the limit at 4 until the rate limit exists, then decide.
4. Accounts that saw a successful login during the run get a forced password reset. Security has the list.
resolution: The CPU limit was raised from 2 to 4 per pod; the 503s stopped at 10:34 and the attack ended at 10:40.
root_cause: A credential-stuffing run sent about 150 login attempts a second; each password check is CPU-heavy by design, so auth-service hit its 2-CPU limit and shed logins with 503 once 64 were in flight per pod.
symptoms: Logins returned 503 through the edge for about 24 minutes while login attempts ran at about ten times the normal rate.
title: Credential stuffing pinned auth-service's CPU
