# Thursday 7 August 2025: the edge stopped being trusted at 04:10

The outage ran from 04:10 to 06:55 UTC on 7 August 2025, which is 165 minutes, and it was a sev1. I was on the team-platform rota, and this is the sequence as it reached me.

What came in first was silence rather than errors. Request rates on every route of edge-gateway fell together at 04:10 and stayed down. Pod 01, pod 02 and pod 03 (edge-gateway-01, edge-gateway-02, edge-gateway-03) all behaved alike, so a single sick pod was ruled out from the first graph. The access logs were quiet too: clients were leaving during the handshake, before Envoy had a request to log.

RB-025 is the reference for the edge certificate. I ran `openssl s_client` against each pod, naming the public host with `-servername`. All three printed `Verify return code: 10 (certificate has expired)`. That code alone suggests a lapsed certificate for our own name. It was not that. Printing the whole chain with `-showcerts` showed the past date sitting on the intermediate the pods hand out, while the certificate for our own name had not run out.

That changed what would help. Renewing our own certificate and restarting the pods would have left clients facing the same dead intermediate. RB-025's fix for this row is to fetch the certificate authority's current chain.

team-platform kept the incident until the end, and by 06:55 handshakes were succeeding again and request rates were back to their usual shape. Which steps were taken is not recorded, and neither is why the expiry of the intermediate was not caught beforehand.

All three pods were affected equally, since each serves the same files, so the load balancer's even spread of connections gave no relief: any connection landed on a pod presenting the same chain. No share of clients and no count of failed connections was kept.

What I would carry forward:

- After a certificate event, read every certificate in the chain a pod serves, not only the one carrying our name.
- A fall in request rates with an empty access log is a handshake problem until shown otherwise.
resolution: team-platform took the incident; clients were connecting normally again by 06:55.
root_cause: The intermediate certificate in the chain served by all three edge pods expired at 04:10, so clients could no longer verify the chain, although the certificate for our own name was still in date.
symptoms: From 04:10 clients abandoned the TLS handshake with edge-gateway-01, edge-gateway-02 and edge-gateway-03, so request rates fell across the routes while the access logs showed no failed requests.
title: All three edge pods served a chain with an expired intermediate

# Postmortem: a night of OOMKilled restarts on orders-api-03

sev2 · 2025-08-09 23:25 to 2025-08-10 11:35 UTC · owner: team-commerce · runbooks: RB-004, RB-005

## The shape of the incident

From 23:25 on the evening of 9 August 2025 until 11:35 the next morning, a stretch of twelve hours and ten minutes, one orders-api pod kept dying. orders-api-03 was terminated by the kernel's memory killer more than once, and each time Kubernetes reported the container's last state as `OOMKilled`. Memory climbed again after the restarts. No restart count was kept, so none is given here.

## Reading the symptom

A container killed for passing its memory limit exits with 137 and the reason `OOMKilled`. A kill after a missed shutdown deadline also exits with 137 but carries another reason, so the reason is the field that tells the cases apart (RB-005). Here the reason was `OOMKilled`.

The incident is a growing JavaScript heap on one pod. RB-004 is the orders-api checklist for that; its standard sets the runtime heap flag, `--max-old-space-size`, to about 75% of the container limit. Why the kills still arrived as `OOMKilled` is not known.

## Evidence that was available

orders-api starts with `--heapsnapshot-signal=SIGUSR2`, so a snapshot can be written from a running pod, and the files land in the working directory `/app`. RB-004 recommends taking one well before the limit, because writing a snapshot costs extra memory. No snapshot from this night exists, which leaves the growing objects and the code that allocated them unidentified.

## Scope and timing

Only orders-api-03 is named for this incident. The service runs on several pods, and what the others did over the night is not known. The only two clock times on record are the start at 23:25 and the end at 11:35, so the individual kills carry no times here. Because the window crosses midnight, the kills fall on two calendar dates, 9 and 10 August.

## Impact

Each kill is abrupt: the container gets no warning, and whatever the pod was serving at that moment goes with it. No failure count or customer figure was kept, and the incident is rated sev2.

## Response

The on-call was on duty for the incident from the start, and the kills had stopped by 11:35. Nothing is written down about a mitigation or about whether a release was suspected.

## Lessons

- The incident ran for twelve hours on one pod without a snapshot being taken, even though the signal flag was already set at startup.
- With no heap evidence, the cause stays at "the heap grew".
- A snapshot early in a climb would have turned this into a finding.
- The pod's own restart counter holds the number of restarts and should be copied into the ticket.
resolution: The on-call took the incident and the kills stopped by 11:35.
root_cause: The JavaScript heap of orders-api-03 grew until the container hit its memory limit and was killed; no heap analysis was recorded, so the growing object and the code path are not known.
symptoms: orders-api-03 was OOMKilled repeatedly between 23:25 and 11:35 the next day, its memory climbing until the container limit was reached each time.
title: orders-api-03 OOMKilled over and over through the night

# Ticket: kafka-02 /var full, GC logs in /var/log/kafka

**Opened:** 2025-08-12 02:30 UTC
**Severity:** sev3
**Host:** kafka-02.prod.internal
**Runbook:** RB-008
**State:** closed 03:45 UTC

## Description

The alert for `/var` usage on kafka-02 fired at 02:30. On this VM `/var` lives on the root disk, so a full `/var` puts every process that writes to the root filesystem at risk, and the first visible sign was `ENOSPC` on writes under `/var`. The word "Kafka" in a disk ticket tends to make people think about topic data, so for the record: the alert is about `/var`, not the data directory `/data/kafka`.

## Comments

**02:36**
`df -h /var` reports 100% used. Looking for what is occupying it before changing anything.

**02:44**
Sizes of the directories under `/var`, largest last: `/var/log/kafka` is far ahead of everything else. That directory holds the broker's garbage-collection logs, and RB-008 has a row for exactly this case on kafka-02.

**02:55**
Reading the row: the GC logs are the thing to rotate here. Whether a rotation setup existed and failed, or never existed, is not something I have confirmed. I will check the logrotate configuration for these logs once the disk has room.

**03:15**
Rotated the GC logs in `/var/log/kafka` and cleared the rotated copies that were not needed. `/var` dropped quickly.

**03:30**
`/var` is under the 80% line that RB-008 sets as the target. GC logging is writing again with no errors showing.

**03:45**
Usage is holding, so I am closing the ticket. The cause is the GC logs in `/var/log/kafka`; why they were allowed to reach this size is still to be looked at.

## Resolution

Rotated the broker GC logs on kafka-02, which freed enough space on `/var`. Only `/var/log/kafka` was worked on; the data volume played no part in this.

## Why this was rated sev3

The alert and the failed writes were both on the root disk of one broker, and the part of the broker that holds Kafka's messages was not what had run out of room. The risk was that other writers on the same root filesystem would start failing too. The runbook's instruction for this host is short: rotate the GC logs and leave the data directory out of it, and that is what was done.

## What ENOSPC meant here

`ENOSPC` says a write had nowhere to go on the filesystem it was aimed at. It does not say which filesystem. On a broker there are two candidates, the data volume and the root disk, and the first job is to find out which is full. Here it was the root disk, because the GC logs live there.

## Follow-ups

- Look at the logrotate setup for `/var/log/kafka` on kafka-02 and decide whether the logs were meant to be rotated and were not.
- Check the same directory on the other two brokers while at it.
- If a rotation file turns out to be missing, put it in config management so a rebuilt host gets it back. This is a conditional follow-up: nothing has confirmed that it is missing.
resolution: The GC logs under /var/log/kafka were rotated, which brought /var back under 80%.
root_cause: The broker's GC logs in /var/log/kafka grew until they filled /var, which shares kafka-02's root disk.
symptoms: The /var disk alert fired for kafka-02 and writes under /var failed with ENOSPC, while the Kafka data directory was not what had filled.
title: kafka-02 /var full of broker GC logs

# Why logins returned 503 on 21 August 2025, in questions

sev3 · 2025-08-21 · 16:05 to 16:40 UTC (35 minutes) · auth-service against auth-db-01 · runbook: RB-024

**What was the user-visible effect?**

From 16:05 logins on `/v1/auth/login` came back `503`. Both pods, auth-service-01 and auth-service-02, could not set up new connections to auth-db-01, and the share of failing logins rose as time passed.

**Why a slow rise and not a cliff?**

Name checking happens at connect time. Pooled connections already open at 16:05 carried on until auth-service's pool let them go: `pool_max_conn_lifetime=1h`, `pool_max_conn_idle_time=30m`, so sooner for the idle ones. Each pod may hold up to 30 pooled connections (`pool_max_conns`), 2 x 30 = 60 across the two pods, and every one that retired could only be replaced by a connection that would be rejected.

**What did the certificate lack?**

auth-service uses `sslmode=verify-full` against the internal CA, which includes a match between the certificate and the name being dialled. The server certificate on auth-db-01 did not carry the name auth-service checks. The names it did contain are not recorded.

**Could it be a repeat of an earlier certificate incident?**

No. It was not an expiry and not a renewed certificate that Postgres had failed to load, which was the cause on 2025-04-08. RB-024 is cited here for the auth-db certificate arrangement.

**Who handled it, and when did the errors stop?**

team-dba took the incident, and logins were normal by 16:40. What ended the failures was not written down.

**How long was it?**

The incident record runs from 16:05 to 16:40, which is 35 minutes. The pool retirement described above is why the failure rate was not constant across those 35 minutes. No count of failed logins exists, which leaves the scale of the impact open. Logins that did succeed in the same window did so on connections that predated the certificate problem.

**What remains unanswered?**

- Which names the auth-db-01 certificate carries, compared with the name auth-service dials.
- How a certificate without the right name came to be installed.
- Whether every older connection had retired by 16:40, or whether some still worked when the errors stopped.
resolution: team-dba took the incident; logins were back to normal by 16:40.
root_cause: The server certificate on auth-db-01 did not carry the name auth-service checks under sslmode=verify-full against the internal CA, so new connections were rejected; the certificate was neither expired nor unloaded.
symptoms: From 16:05 new database connections from auth-service-01 and auth-service-02 to auth-db-01 failed and logins returned 503, while connections opened earlier kept working until they aged out.
title: Logins returned 503 because auth-db-01's certificate lacked the name auth-service checks

# The 23 August 2025 slow feature store, asked and answered

sev3 · 03:35 to 04:00 UTC · store: redis-features-01 · seen in: fraud-scorer-01, payments-api · runbook: RB-006

**What showed up first?**

At 03:35 fraud-scorer-01 started logging `FRD-W118`, the warning for slow feature reads from the store (RB-006 pairs it with `PAYAPI-W0310` on the payments side). Soon after, payments-api logged `PAYAPI-W0310`. Both kept appearing until 04:00.

**Two services complain. Where is the fault?**

On redis-features-01. The feature store is one machine with nothing to fail over to, so when it drags, every reader drags with it. The scorer and payments-api are only where the delay becomes visible.

**What made the store slow?**

Key scans. One of them can occupy Redis's single serving thread for a while, and ordinary lookups line up behind it. RB-006 names big scans among the usual reasons for this store to slow down; a background save is also on its list, and nothing here points to one.

**Why did the scans matter to payments?**

Payments-api consumes the scorer's output, and the scorer consumes the store's. A delay at the bottom of that chain reaches the top as a warning from each service in turn, which is the order in which the two codes appeared.

**Who ran the scans?**

Not known. The client and the purpose were not recorded.

**Was it the memory problem RB-006 is titled after?**

That runbook is about memory creep in the scorer, and it treats a slow feature store as what feeds the creep. It is cited for the link between the store and `FRD-W118`. Whether memory in the scorer moved during these minutes was not recorded.

**How big was it?**

From 03:35 to 04:00 is 25 minutes, rated sev3. How many payments were touched by `PAYAPI-W0310` was not counted.

**When was it over?**

The risk on-call took the incident, and the warnings were gone by 04:00. What stopped the scans was not recorded.

**What should change?**

- Learn which client issues the scans, and have it page through keys in small steps or run off this node.
- Put the store's latency on the first dashboard the risk on-call opens for a `PAYAPI-W0310` page.
- Keep the scorer's `FRD-W118` count beside it.
resolution: The risk on-call took the incident and both warnings had stopped by 04:00; what ended the scans was not recorded.
root_cause: Key scans on redis-features-01 made the single feature store slow, so feature reads from fraud-scorer-01 ran late, which showed as FRD-W118 and PAYAPI-W0310; who ran the scans is not known.
symptoms: fraud-scorer-01 logged FRD-W118 and payments-api logged PAYAPI-W0310 for 25 minutes in the small hours of a Saturday.

# #platform-oncall digest: SERVFAIL from internal-dns-01, 2 September 2025

sev2, 11:20 to 11:35 UTC, 15 minutes. The thread opened with failed lookups on notification-worker-01 at 11:20 and closed at 11:35 with clean lookups. Messages are grouped below by who wrote them, not by clock, because no times were kept between those two. RB-020 is the runbook that came up.

Why the zone failed to load was not established.

**Background posted in the thread**

internal-dns is two VMs running CoreDNS, each holding its own copy of the `prod.internal` zone, and both are authoritative for it. Records carry a 60 s TTL.

**Severity**

The incident carried sev2 from 11:20 to 11:35, a span of 15 minutes, with notification-worker-01 as the host that showed the symptom.

**Closing message**

At 11:35 lookups from notification-worker-01 were clean again. team-platform handled the incident to the end. RB-020 has its own entry for a SERVFAIL from one server and the cluster resolver's cache keeps answers for at most 30 seconds, per the runbook; nothing says that entry was followed, or what ended the errors, and no count of failed lookups was kept.
resolution: team-platform took the incident; lookups from notification-worker-01 were clean again by 11:35.
root_cause: The prod.internal zone failed to load on internal-dns-01, so that server answered SERVFAIL; pods reach it only some of the time because the cluster resolver picks an upstream at random. Why the zone failed to load is not recorded.
symptoms: From 11:20 some name lookups from notification-worker-01 failed with SERVFAIL, because internal-dns-01 could not answer for prod.internal names.

# 8 September 2025: ledger-service-01 and a pool that would not empty

Running log of a Monday morning. Rated sev2, times in UTC. Window 10:05 to 11:35, which is 90 minutes. Runbooks cited: RB-001 and RB-012.

## Clock

```
10:05  start. LEDGER-W210 on ledger-service-01: Hikari pool above 90% active.
10:05+ callers begin to queue for a connection; ones that wait the full 30 s
       get Hikari's timeout, and payments-api starts receiving 503.
....   (no other times were kept)
       RB-001 opened first, because that warning order points at the JVM.
       RB-012 opened for the connection budget.
       Slow queries on ledger-db-01 are what hold the connections.
11:35  end. Errors on the ledger path stopped.
```

## Reading the log

LEDGER-W210 means the Hikari pool on ledger-service-01 is more than 90% in use, and its limit is 20 connections. Once all 20 were checked out by calls waiting on ledger-db-01, the next caller queued. After 30 seconds Hikari gave up with its message that the request timed out after 30000ms, and payments-api received a 503 from the ledger. The chain is slow database work, a full pool, timed-out callers, and a 503 upstream.

RB-001 was the first runbook opened because LEDGER-W210 usually arrives ahead of a 503, and the card warns that this ordering tempts people to treat it as a database problem when it may be the JVM. Here the slow queries on ledger-db-01 were the holders of the connections. RB-012 supplied the budget: ledger-service's two pods hold 2 x 20 = 40 of the 197 usable slots on ledger-db (200 minus 3), so a bigger pool was not a remedy.

## Unrecorded

- Which statements were slow, and why, was not recorded.
- Whether other ledger-service instances were affected was not recorded.
- What ended the slow queries was not recorded. The ledger on-call took the incident and the errors had stopped by 11:35.

## Carried forward

- Alert when callers start waiting for a connection (pending above 0).
- When LEDGER-W210 fires, look at the database sessions before the JVM.
resolution: The ledger on-call took the incident and the errors had stopped by 11:35; what ended the slow queries was not recorded.
root_cause: Slow queries on ledger-db-01 kept ledger-service-01's HikariCP connections checked out, so the 20-connection pool stayed full and callers waited until their time ran out.
symptoms: ledger-service-01 logged LEDGER-W210, then Hikari timeouts after 30000ms, and payments-api received 503 from it until 11:35.

# Refused feature-store writes on 9 September 2025: questions and answers

Risk and platform, sev3, 11:20 to 13:05 UTC. RB-019 was the reference.

**What did we see first?**

At 11:20 both fraud-scorer-01 and fraud-scorer-02 started logging `FRD-E140`. Behind it, redis-features-01 was turning down writes with `MISCONF`, so the per-card counters fraud-scorer maintains stopped moving.

**What does `FRD-E140` mean for the business?**

fraud-scorer increments a velocity counter, with an expiry, on every score it computes. While the writes were refused those counters could not be updated, so they went stale and stayed that way until writes recovered. Scores computed in between were working from counters that were out of date, which is why the code is worth watching even when the service looks otherwise healthy.

**Memory looked fine. Why did the node refuse writes anyway?**

Redis held about 14 GB on a 32 GB VM, comfortably inside its own limits. The refusals came from a different place: the node's snapshot attempts were failing, and Redis stops accepting writes when that happens. The Redis log carried `Can't save in background: fork: Cannot allocate memory`.

**Why would a fork fail on a machine with that much free memory?**

A hardening change from team-platform had switched redis-features-01 to strict memory accounting (`vm.overcommit_memory = 2`, ratio 80). With no swap, that caps total commitments at 32 GB x 80% + 0 = 25.6 GB. A snapshot forks a child that is billed about like its parent, so 14 GB plus 14 GB asks for roughly 28 GB, more than 25.6 GB. The machine had room; the accounting rule did not.

**How did it end?**

The setting went back to 1, a new snapshot was started by hand and finished, and writes were accepted again. The `FRD-E140` lines from both scorers stopped, and we closed at 13:05. Almost two hours passed between first symptom and fix, since the cause sat in the OS settings rather than in anything Redis reported about memory.

**What changes afterwards?**

The sysctl on the host was a patch. The hardening baseline that applied strict mode has to stop doing so, otherwise it can come back. That is with team-platform.

**What is still open?**

Whether other hosts picked up the same baseline value has not been looked at.
resolution: vm.overcommit_memory was set back to 1, a fresh BGSAVE succeeded, and writes were accepted again by 13:05.
root_cause: A baseline change set vm.overcommit_memory=2 with ratio 80 on redis-features-01; with Redis near 14 GB the background-save fork exceeded a 25.6 GB commit limit and failed, so Redis stopped accepting writes.
symptoms: redis-features-01 began refusing writes with MISCONF from 11:20, and fraud-scorer-01 and fraud-scorer-02 logged FRD-E140 because their velocity counters stopped updating.
title: redis-features-01 refused writes after a strict overcommit setting

# 19 September 2025, overnight: fraud-scorer-02 and the restart that did not stick

Clock log kept by the night on-call. sev2. UTC throughout. Runbooks used: RB-005, RB-006.

## Clock (UTC)

```
03:40  payments fallback alert: PAYAPI-W0310 well above its night-time level. Paged.
03:47  on-call starts on the payments side, assuming payments-api itself is slow.
       Its own handlers look normal; the time is spent waiting on fraud scores.
03:58  fraud-scorer: fraud-scorer-02 has a long latency tail. FRD-W118 present.
04:05  RB-005 first, to see if pods are dying. describe pod: Last State empty,
       no terminations. Memory panel: fraud-scorer-02 rising steadily since
       about 03:40 at flat traffic. Growth, not a limit sized too small.
04:14  RB-006: FRD-W118 counted per pod. Almost all of it on fraud-scorer-02.
04:22  redis-cli --latency on redis-features-01: spikes, but irregular. Not an
       obvious cause at a glance.
04:38  memory on fraud-scorer-02 still climbing, rss about 2,860 MiB of 3,072.
       Decision: restart now to keep headroom, keep looking
       for the cause in parallel.
04:50  rollout restart issued for the fraud-scorer Deployment.
05:02  new pods serving. fraud-scorer-02 back near baseline. PAYAPI-W0310 drops.
05:20  FRD-W118 back on fraud-scorer-02, and memory is rising again from the
       new baseline. The restart reset the curve; it did not stop it.
05:31  escalated to team-platform for redis-features.
05:48  --latency again: spikes still coming, and closer together than at 04:22.
       Per RB-006 the usual culprits here are heavy key scans or BGSAVE;
       team-platform asked to look from the store's side.
06:20  latency samples on redis-features-01 ease and go flat.
06:22  FRD-W118 stops on fraud-scorer-02. Memory flat but still high.
06:30  second rollout restart, this time with the store answering normally.
06:41  both pods at baseline. PAYAPI-W0310 gone.
06:55  holding steady; resolved.
```

## Two restarts, one cause

RB-006 lists the restart as a stopgap, and this night showed what that word means. The 04:50 restart was the right call for the memory: fraud-scorer-02 stood at about 2,860 MiB of its 3,072 MiB limit at 04:38, and the restart pulled it back. But the cache inside each worker grows whenever reads from redis-features are slow, and at 05:02 the reads were still slow. Within 18 minutes of the new pods taking traffic the warnings were back and the curve was climbing again.

The second restart held because the store was already answering normally when it ran. Waiting for the store before refreshing the pods is the order to follow when the store is still misbehaving.

## Why the cause took two hours

The 04:22 latency check did show the problem, but it looked irregular, and the on-call did not trust it on its own. The scorer saw bursts of slow reads, not a wall, and bursts are easy to wave away at night. Only the second look at 05:48 made it clear the store was the thing to wait on. Starting on the payments side cost the first part of the night too.

## Why sev2

From 03:40 payments-api logged `PAYAPI-W0310` well above its night-time level, and the first restart did nothing about the slow store behind it.

## Carry-forward

- Treat irregular `--latency` spikes on redis-features as real when `FRD-W118` is high.
- Note the rss figure at each restart, so the next on-call can see how fast the cache refills.
- Keep the "fix the store, then restart" order in the team's notes for the next one.
resolution: A first restart at 04:50 only reset the growth; once redis-features latency eased at 06:20, a second rolling restart at 06:30 held and the incident closed at 06:55.
root_cause: redis-features-01 stayed slow for hours; fraud-scorer's in-process feature cache on fraud-scorer-02 grew for as long as the reads stayed slow.
symptoms: Overnight, payments-api fell back to static fraud rules (PAYAPI-W0310); fraud-scorer-02 logged FRD-W118 and its memory climbed, came down after a restart, then climbed again.
title: fraud-scorer-02 grew back after the first restart: a slow night on redis-features

# Postmortem: the missing database record, 19 September 2025

Authors: team-platform. Severity: sev2. Timestamps are UTC. Window: 20:25 to 21:40, 75 minutes. Runbooks cited: RB-020, RB-027.

## Summary

A zone-file push on the evening of 19 September 2025 left internal-dns-02 serving a version of `prod.internal` missing the record catalog-api-02 needs for its database. The other internal-dns server's copy of the zone still carried it. Whether a lookup worked therefore depended on which server the cluster resolver asked, and catalog-api-02 saw failures that came and went for 75 minutes. The tool finished reporting 0 failed hosts, so the push raised no alarm by itself.

## Impact

The symptom surfaced in catalog-api rather than in internal-dns. Each time catalog-api-02 wanted its database address and got `NXDOMAIN`, that attempt failed; a later attempt might reach the other server and work. The result was an uneven error pattern on one instance, easy to mistake for a database fault. No request count was recorded for the window.

## Why it came and went

Pods ask the cluster CoreDNS, which forwards `prod.internal` queries to one internal-dns server picked at random and caches the reply, `NXDOMAIN` included, for no more than 30 seconds (`cache 30`).

For catalog-api-02 that produced a series of short windows. A window opened by a query to the intact server carried the address. A window opened by a query to internal-dns-02 carried `NXDOMAIN` for up to half a minute. Both servers were up; one of them simply held less.

## Why the push looked fine

In September 2025 the tool's only verdict on a host was whether `systemctl restart` succeeded. Nothing in that sequence compared the records a server held against the records it should hold. CoreDNS restarted, read the file and served it, with the record missing. Nothing flagged it.

RB-027, the runbook for VM config pushes, was an obvious first read. It is about services that exit soon after systemd reports a start, and it names the `kafka` unit as `Type=simple` to make the point. Nothing suggested coredns had exited; the open question was what internal-dns-02 served.

## How it was narrowed down

- The errors in catalog-api-02 shared one cause: the name query for the database host was answered `NXDOMAIN`. Failures alternated with successes, which suggested the two servers disagreed, not that the name was gone everywhere.
- RB-020 reads intermittent pod failures as two servers disagreeing, and its test is to question each server directly and compare answers and SOA serials.
- The push that landed at 20:25 fitted the start of the errors.

Why the pushed file lacked the record was not recorded.

## Resolution

team-platform took the incident, and the lookups stopped failing by 21:40. Which step ended the failures was not recorded. RB-020 has a remedy for a missing record; whether it was applied is not recorded.

## Lessons

1. A clean exit from the tool says the process restarted. It says nothing about which names the server can answer.
2. Random forwarding across two servers makes a one-server fault look flaky from inside the cluster, which slows the recognition of a disagreement.
3. RB-027 helped to rule out a daemon fault; the content question sat with RB-020.

## Proposed follow-ups

- Give catalog-api's connection errors the failing name and the resolver's answer, so the next page points at DNS instead of the database.
- Have the push summary show, for each server, the SOA serial and how many records it now holds.
resolution: team-platform took the incident; the lookups stopped failing by 21:40.
root_cause: A zone-file push left internal-dns-02 serving a prod.internal file that lacked the catalog database record, so the cluster resolver got NXDOMAIN whenever it happened to ask that server; the push tool still ended with a report of 0 failed hosts.
symptoms: From 20:25 catalog-api-02 intermittently failed to reach its database as its name query for the catalog database record was answered NXDOMAIN, while other queries kept working.
title: catalog-api-02 lost its database name for part of an evening

# Abandoned handshakes on edge-gateway-03, 21 September 2025

Service edge-gateway, sev4, from 10:45 to 15:05 UTC (260 minutes). Runbook: RB-025.

```
10:45  handshakes from one client start being abandoned; edge-gateway-03 logs them
15:05  closed; the cause was the client's own device clock, and the edge stays as it was
```

Only two moments are on record, so the timeline has two entries. The 260 minutes run from the first abandoned handshake to the close, which is four hours and twenty minutes.

## Where the log lines came from

edge-gateway-03 wrote the log lines for the broken-off handshakes, and its certificate was examined. A wrong clock fails against every pod the client reaches, so the pod that holds the log says nothing about the route the client took.

## Cause and decision

The clock on the client's device was wrong, so the client judged our certificate against the wrong date. RB-025 sets that case apart from faults in what the edge serves: one caller affected, others fine. After the examination of the certificate on edge-gateway-03, the edge was left alone. No certificate file, Secret or pod was touched, and the incident ended at 15:05 with nothing changed on our side.

## The edge as it stood

Callers reach the gateway on port 443. Its certificate comes from a public CA, lives in a Secret and is mounted as files into every pod; Envoy reads the files at start, so a renewal needs a restart of the Deployment. None of that was touched during the 260 minutes, and the incident record names no change to any of it.

## Scale

The incident carried sev4. One caller is on record as affected, and no count of abandoned handshakes was kept; RB-025 describes this case as one client failing while the others connect.

## Unrecorded

Who the caller was, which device it used and what error it showed. No reading of the device clock was taken either.
resolution: Nothing was changed at the edge; the matter was closed at 15:05 as a client-side problem.
root_cause: The clock on the client's own device was wrong, so the client judged the edge's certificate against the wrong date; the edge itself was not at fault.
symptoms: From 10:45 handshakes from one client were abandoned and logged on edge-gateway-03, and the certificate presented on that pod was examined.

# A change-feed slot kept WAL piling up on payments-db-01

sev2 · 2025-09-25 · 04:10 to 07:30 UTC · cause: disk_full · affected: payments-db · runbook: RB-007

| Who | When (UTC) | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| payments-db-01 | 04:10 | The alert on retained WAL above 50 GB fired and the incident was opened. The volume had not filled. |
| on-call | after 04:10 | Listed the replication slots. `cdc_payments` was inactive and holding the most WAL. |
| team-dba | during the incident | Dropping a slot needs the DBA lead's approval, so removal was not a quick option. How the slot stopped holding WAL is not recorded in the ticket. |
| payments-db-01 | before 07:30 | `cdc_payments` no longer held old WAL, and a manual checkpoint let Postgres delete the segments nothing needed. |
| payments-db-01 | 07:30 | Retained WAL back to its usual size. Closed. |

## Why the alert threshold matters

On this volume the free space is about 95 GB on a normal day, while the server's own cap on slot WAL is 200 GB. A stuck slot would therefore fill the disk before the cap acted, which makes the 50 GB alert the working guard. It did its job here: the disk never filled and no out-of-space failure occurred.

## Who was touched

| Component | Effect |
|---|---|
| payments-db-01 | Carried extra WAL from 04:10 to 07:30 but kept running. |
| ledger reconciliation pipeline | The feed behind `cdc_payments` was the consumer that stopped. |

## Open questions

- Why `cdc_payments` stopped advancing at all. The incident record does not say, and the first place to ask is the owner of the reconciliation pipeline that reads it.
- How long the slot had been inactive before the alert fired. The alert measures retained size, not inactivity, so those two moments may differ.
- Whether the slot was kept or dropped at the end. Nothing in the record states either.

## Follow-ups

- Tell the pipeline owner when the slot first goes inactive, not only when retained WAL reaches 50 GB.
- Write down in the ticket how the slot was released, since this one did not record it.
resolution: The slot stopped holding WAL and a checkpoint let Postgres remove the old segments; the incident closed at 07:30.
root_cause: The logical slot cdc_payments stopped advancing, so payments-db-01 kept every WAL segment from the slot's last confirmed position onward.
symptoms: The retained-WAL alert on payments-db-01 fired when an inactive slot was keeping WAL segments on disk; the data volume never filled.
title: Stalled change-feed slot held WAL on the payments primary

# Postmortem: reservations queries slowed by table bloat on inventory-db-01

sev2 · 2025-10-09 · 03:50 to 04:25 UTC · owner: team-commerce · runbook: RB-015

## Incident record

Checkout depends on a stock reservation, and from 03:50 to 04:25, which is 35 minutes, reservations took too long. inventory-service-02 logged `INV-E220` each time a reservation timed out, and orders-api logged `ORD-5003` against the same calls.

The database behind them, inventory-db-01, was answering, only slowly. Nothing recorded shows it refusing connections.

## Impact

Checkout reaches inventory through the reservation call, so checkouts that needed a reservation during the 35 minutes were slow or failed. The records hold no count of affected orders or customers, and the incident is rated sev2.

## What the slowness was

The `reservations` table is the inventory table that reservation queries read and write. A Postgres table that has gone through many updates and deletes carries leftover dead row versions until cleanup reclaims them. That extra material is table bloat: a query has to read past it, so the same lookup costs more pages than it should. On inventory-db-01 the reservations table had reached that condition, and reservation queries paid for it.

Its size, its dead-row count and whether a cleanup ran during the window were not captured, so no such figures appear here. What produced the bloat is not known either.

## Evidence on hand

The error logs are the main evidence. inventory-service-02 is the instance whose log is on record, and its `INV-E220` lines mark the reservations that timed out. Both codes began together at 03:50 and both had stopped by 04:25. RB-015 is the runbook for slow stock reservations and covers this path. No query plan, table statistics or session listing from the window made it into the record, which is why the explanation above rests on the table and the error codes alone.

## Reading the two codes together

The codes sit at two ends of one call. `INV-E220` comes from the inventory side and says a reservation timed out; `ORD-5003` comes from the orders side and says its call did not complete. Seeing both begin at 03:50 and end by 04:25 ties them to the same stretch of slow reservations rather than to two separate faults.

## Response

team-commerce took the incident, and by 04:25 reservations were completing again. Nothing is recorded about what was done to the table.

## Lessons

1. The first signal anyone has on record is the reservation timeout code, not a warning from the table itself.
2. The failure also surfaced on the orders side, a hop away from the table that caused it, so the inventory log was where the slow dependency showed.
3. Table size and dead-row counts taken at the time would show how large the bloat was.
resolution: team-commerce took the incident at sev2 and the errors had stopped by 04:25; the step that ended them was not recorded.
root_cause: Table bloat on inventory-db-01 made queries against the reservations table slow; how the bloat built up is not known.
symptoms: From 03:50 inventory-service-02 logged INV-E220 for stock reservations that timed out, and orders-api reported ORD-5003 on checkout.
title: Bloated reservations table slowed stock holds

# Postmortem: the broker that ran out of root disk, not data disk

**Date:** Saturday 11 October 2025
**Window:** 11:55 to 13:40 UTC (105 minutes)
**Severity:** sev3
**Host:** kafka-01.prod.internal
**Runbooks used:** RB-009, then RB-008
**Written by:** team-platform

## Where we started

At 11:55 the log agent on kafka-01 began sending `ENOSPC` errors about its own bookkeeping files. Shortly after, the broker's files under `/var/log/kafka` stopped getting new lines. Our first reaction was the obvious one for a Kafka host: a broker that is out of space must be out of space for its partitions. That instinct shaped the next 40 minutes.

## Ruling out the data volume

We opened RB-009 and did its first step on every broker: `df -h /data/kafka`. All three looked ordinary and close to each other, which is what replicated data should look like. kafka-01 was not ahead of its peers. If the partition volume had been the problem we would also have expected the broker to stop and producers to start complaining; neither had happened. The broker was still leading and following partitions as usual, and while we worked we saw no under-replication alert.

The `df` numbers settled it quickly, but we did not trust them at first and went on to RB-009's second step, summing partition sizes per topic from `kafka-log-dirs.sh`, to see whether kafka-01 held anything unusual. It did not. Only then did we accept that the data disk was fine. That told us the space problem was on the other filesystem, the root disk, where `/var` lives on our VMs. We stopped the retention work before it began. We did not shorten any topic, which matters because RB-009 is explicit that cutting retention below a consumer's lag throws away unread messages.

## Finding the real consumer of space

Switching to RB-008, `df -h /var` showed the root filesystem completely full. We sized the directories under `/var` and found two candidates worth checking:

- `/var/log/kafka`, where the broker's GC logs are written. Rotation there was working; the directory was a modest size.
- `/var/log/journal`, which was by far the largest.

`journalctl --disk-usage` matched what `du` said. The journald configuration on kafka-01 had no size limit at all. Whatever the broker and the OS had logged since the VM was built was still on disk.

## What we changed

1. 12:41 · `sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=500M` on kafka-01. The root disk dropped back to a comfortable level within seconds.
2. 12:47 · the log agent's `ENOSPC` errors stopped and broker lines in `/var/log/kafka` started updating again.
3. 12:58 · added `SystemMaxUse=500M` to `/etc/systemd/journald.conf` and restarted `systemd-journald`. The disk-usage report afterwards sat under the new cap.
4. 13:40 · after watching usage stay level, we closed the incident.

We did not restart the broker, and we did not touch anything under `/data/kafka`.

## Effect on users

We saw no producer or consumer errors during the window. The broker's data path is on its own volume, so partition writes carried on. What we did lose is local logging on kafka-01 between 11:55 and 12:47: lines the broker tried to write to `/var/log/kafka` in that window may be incomplete, and journal entries from that period could not be stored. If anyone needs broker logs for that stretch, they will have gaps.

## Why it took us a while

About 40 minutes went on the data-volume hypothesis: from 11:55 until 12:35, when we moved on to the root disk. Looking back, the clues were there early. The `ENOSPC` came from the log agent, not from Kafka, and the broker was still healthy. A full `/data/kafka` looks very different. Checking RB-009's first step was cheap and worth doing. Going on to per-topic sizes after `df` had already cleared the volume is where the time went; `df -h /var` in parallel would have pointed at the root disk much sooner.

## What went well

- Nobody deleted files by hand in either `/data/kafka` or `/var/log/journal`.
- No topic retention was changed on the strength of a wrong guess.

## Proposal

Add a line to the on-call notes: on a broker, an `ENOSPC` that comes from the log agent points at `/var`, not at the partition volume.
resolution: Vacuumed the journal to 500M and set SystemMaxUse=500M in /etc/systemd/journald.conf on kafka-01; broker data was left untouched.
root_cause: kafka-01 had never received a journald size limit, so the systemd journal in /var/log/journal grew on the root disk until it was full.
symptoms: kafka-01's root disk reached 100% and local writes under /var failed with ENOSPC; the broker kept serving and /data/kafka had normal headroom.
title: kafka-01 root disk exhausted while its data volume stayed healthy

# The Wednesday evening catalog-api could not get a connection

On 15 October 2025, from 21:30 until 22:10 UTC, product requests to catalog-api that needed the database stopped coming back. The incident is rated sev3. It lasted 40 minutes, and the instances involved were catalog-api-01 and catalog-api-02.

Product requests that needed catalog-db were the ones affected. For those, the edge gave up with a `504` once its 15-second route timeout ran out.

## How the pools work, and why they filled

Each catalog-api instance uses a SQLAlchemy QueuePool of 10 connections, with room to overflow by 5 more. That is 15 per instance, and with two instances 2 x 15 = 30 connections for the whole service. The pool is a queue: a request that finds all 15 in use waits for one to come back, and after 30 seconds it gives up with the pool's own timeout error, which says the limit of size 10 with overflow 5 was reached.

That 30-second wait is longer than the edge's 15-second route timeout. So a request that waited for a connection typically drew a `504` from the edge at 15 seconds, and the pool timeout followed in the service log about 15 seconds later (30 - 15), after the edge had already answered.

What kept the connections busy was slow work on catalog-db. A query that normally returns quickly took long enough that each connection stayed checked out far beyond its usual short stay. With 30 connections in total, it took only a modest number of those slow queries running together to use up the whole supply. The query was not recorded, and neither was the reason it was slow.

## What people did

The edge alerts on its `504` rate. RB-028 is the runbook for catalog-api pool trouble, so it was the one cited. It is about a migration waiting on a lock, and nothing in this incident was a migration.

The catalog on-call took the incident. The pool errors and the `504`s had stopped by 22:10, when it was closed. What ended the slow query was not recorded.

## What stays open

- The identity of the slow query and the cause of its slowness.
- Whether the 30-second pool wait should stay longer than the edge's 15 seconds. 
- An alert on pool wait time per instance, ahead of the edge's `504` rate.
resolution: The catalog on-call took the incident and the errors had stopped by 22:10; what ended the slow query was not recorded.
root_cause: A slow query on catalog-db kept connections checked out, so the 30 connections of catalog-api's two QueuePools (10 plus 5 overflow, per instance) were all in use and later requests waited for one.
symptoms: catalog-api-01 and catalog-api-02 logged QueuePool timeouts and the edge returned 504 on product requests that missed the cache.
title: catalog-api pools stuck behind a slow catalog-db query

# Handoff: ledger-service CPU, Thursday 23 October 2025

**ledger-service-01 and ledger-service-02 · CPU high with LEDGER-E455 in the logs · sev2 · 16:40 to 17:55 UTC · RB-001 · closed**

Short version: Kafka stopped accepting our publishes, and ledger-service's retry threads kept hammering a queue that could not drain. The CPU alarm was a side effect; the trigger was upstream of us. It ended when the outage did.

## State you inherit

- Both ledger-service-01 and ledger-service-02 are healthy and `LEDGER-E455` has stopped.
- Publishes to the ledger topic succeed and the retry queue is empty. CPU on both instances is back to its usual level.

## What the incident looked like

From 16:40 both instances ran hot together, which pointed away from a single-instance cause. Several `ledger-retry-*` threads were busy in their retry loop, and each entry that could not be published produced a `LEDGER-E455` line before going back on the queue. That is the retry spin: the worker polls again immediately instead of waiting, so CPU climbs for as long as publishes keep failing. RB-001 was my guide for telling it apart from garbage collection and from a heavy batch.

The way out was on the Kafka side. Once publishes were accepted again, the queue drained by itself and the threads settled. By 17:55 it was over.

## What I do not have

I have no cause for the Kafka refusal. Ask whoever owns that side.

## For the next shift

- The retry worker should pause between attempts, with the delay growing, rather than polling flat out. A Kafka outage can cause this again while the worker polls flat out.
- If asked for evidence, the thread dumps from both pods show the retry threads in the same loop.
resolution: Once the Kafka outage ended, publishes succeeded, the retry queue drained and the spinning stopped; CPU was back to normal by 17:55.
root_cause: Kafka was refusing publishes, and the ledger-retry threads re-polled their queue with no backoff, so each instance spun on the retry queue instead of waiting.
symptoms: CPU on ledger-service-01 and ledger-service-02 climbed from 16:40 while LEDGER-E455 was logged for every entry that could not be published.
title: Retry threads on both ledger-service instances burned CPU during a Kafka outage

# The cache that was there but not ready

Early on Sunday 26 October 2025 I was carrying the catalog pager. What follows is my account of a short sev3, which began at 02:50 UTC and had ended by 03:10.

The alert that reached me was about catalog-api, not Redis. catalog-api-02.prod.internal had begun emitting `CAT-E301`, our code for "couldn't get this from the cache, fetching it from catalog-db instead". In my experience that code had always meant an unreachable Redis box, so I opened RB-017 already picturing a dead VM and a failover.

That picture was wrong. I found no timeouts and no refused connections. Each failed cache lookup from catalog-api-02 came back from redis-cache-02.prod.internal with one word: `LOADING`. So Redis was alive, listening and replying; its reply simply said it was still pulling its dataset off disk and couldn't hand out keys yet. That only happens shortly after a Redis process starts, so redis-cache-02 had restarted. Why it restarted, I don't know, and this account doesn't speculate.

Which left me one real responsibility. When cached product data is unavailable, the thing at risk is the database behind it, since nearly all catalog reads are normally answered by Redis and every miss becomes a SQL query. Following the checklist, I kept two graphs open side by side: catalog-db CPU and the rate of `CAT-E301`. Database work went up, as you'd expect, yet it never got near the threshold at which RB-017 asks for escalation. Running out of sessions was never a concern either, because catalog-api's connection pools are bounded.

I left Redis alone. A process in the middle of loading is minutes away from healthy, and restarting it would only reset that clock. The checklist also rules out manual promotion, and nothing here tempted me toward it.

Shortly before 03:00 the `LOADING` answers ceased. catalog-api-02's lookups started succeeding, and `CAT-E301` went quiet. Redis came back with little useful content, so catalog-db kept absorbing extra reads for a while as popular products were cached again. That warm-up behaved just as the runbook predicts: hits rose, database CPU eased back to normal, and at 03:10 nothing looked unusual anymore. Twenty minutes, first error to finish.

What I'm keeping from this:

- `CAT-E301` says the cache didn't deliver. It doesn't say the cache host is gone. Had I read the wrapped Redis error before anything else, I'd have skipped some pointless checks.
- With a cache that's reloading, the job is to wait and keep watching the database. That's the core of RB-017's catalog-db section in practice.
- What triggered the restart of redis-cache-02 remains unknown.
resolution: No intervention on Redis was needed: once the load completed, catalog-api-02's cache reads succeeded, CAT-E301 stopped and catalog-db load came back down as the cache warmed.
root_cause: redis-cache-02 had restarted and was reading its dataset back into memory; until it finished it answered commands with LOADING, which catalog-api treats as the cache being unavailable.
symptoms: catalog-api-02 got LOADING replies from redis-cache-02 and logged CAT-E301, sending its product reads through to catalog-db for about 20 minutes.
title: catalog-api-02 read past a Redis that was still loading

# Ten minutes of failed card payments, 5 November 2025

I'm on team-payments, and the sev1 on Wednesday morning was my release. It ran from
09:05 to 09:15 UTC. This is what happened, as I saw it.

I shipped a new card-processor-proxy release that morning. The new pods passed their readiness
checks, so as far as the rollout could tell, everything was fine. It wasn't. From 09:05,
payments that went through the new version of the proxy failed, and payments-api logged
`PAYAPI-E1107` for each one whose attempts were all used up.

The alert on the payment error rate fired at 09:08. The failures began with my release, so
that is where I looked first. At 09:10 I ran
`kubectl -n payments rollout undo deploy/card-processor-proxy` and watched both instances,
card-processor-proxy-01 as well as card-processor-proxy-02, go back to the previous version.
As the old version took over again,
`PAYAPI-E1107` tailed off and then stopped. I watched the error rate stay flat and closed the
incident at 09:15, 10 minutes after the first failure.

Ten minutes is short for a sev1, but each of those minutes meant card payments failing. What kept
it short was having a lever that needed no understanding of the bug: the previous version had
been serving payments without trouble right up to 09:05, and an undo puts it back. I would rather
have that lever ready than try to be clever under pressure.

What I don't know yet is which change in the release broke the calls to the processor. Reading
the diff is today's job; until then the cause stays open.

What I'd change:

1. A pod passing its readiness check proved nothing about calls to the processor. Making a
   pod complete one test call before it counts as ready would have stopped this release before
   it took real payments.
2. A pause in the rollout after the first new instance, long enough to watch `PAYAPI-E1107`,
   would have limited how many payments met the bad version.
3. Proxy releases go out off-peak, with a second person watching the payment error rate.
4. The rollback was the right lever and it was quick. I'd like the undo command in our release
   checklist, so whoever is shipping doesn't have to look it up with failures climbing.
resolution: The release was rolled back at 09:10; once the previous version was serving again the failures stopped, and the incident closed at 09:15.
root_cause: A regression in that morning's card-processor-proxy release; payments handled by the new version failed.
symptoms: From 09:05 payments-api logged PAYAPI-E1107 as card payments failed through the newly released card-processor-proxy on card-processor-proxy-01 and card-processor-proxy-02.
title: My card proxy release failed payments for ten minutes

From: evening on-call, team-risk. To: night on-call. Written at 21:25 UTC as the incident closed.

Resolved. Sev3, open from 17:25 to 21:25. fraud-scorer-02 is running clean after a rolling restart; no `FRD-W118` since 19:52.

## What happened tonight

- 17:25 First `FRD-W118` on fraud-scorer-02, then `PAYAPI-W0310` from payments-api.
- 17:58 fraud-scorer-02 restarted. Per RB-005 I read `Last State` rather than trusting the exit code: `OOMKilled`, exit 137. Not an eviction.
- 18:10 RB-006: `redis-cli --latency` on redis-features-01 showed spikes. They eased at 18:24.

- 19:41 Second `OOMKilled` on fraud-scorer-02.
- 19:52 Store latency eased to normal, warnings stopped.
- 20:40 After watching for a third slow stretch that did not come, rolling restart of the fraud-scorer Deployment so both pods start empty.
- 21:25 Flat since; closed.

## Why it reached the limit this time

The memory budget is tight. `WEB_CONCURRENCY` is unset, so the pod runs one worker per visible core: 16 on its node. At about 150 MiB per warm worker that is 2,400 MiB before any cache growth, inside a 3,072 MiB limit. That leaves 672 MiB for the feature cache, and each slow stretch on redis-features filled it. The memory panel shows the same shape both times: level, then a straight climb from the first spikes to the kill.

## For the night

- Watch "Container memory (working set)" for fraud-scorer-02. A climb with `FRD-W118` alongside it means the store is slow again.
- If redis-features slows again and the climb returns, restart before the limit, not after.
- Do not raise the memory limit tonight. RB-005's point stands: it would hide the growth, not stop it.
- The 20:40 restart left both pods at baseline, so any climb from here is new growth, not leftover.
resolution: After the second slow stretch eased, fraud-scorer was given a rolling restart; memory stayed flat to the end of the shift and the incident was closed at 21:25.
root_cause: Two slow stretches on redis-features-01 delayed feature reads; each time, the in-process feature cache on fraud-scorer-02 grew past the room left above its 16 warm workers and the pod hit its 3 GiB limit.
symptoms: fraud-scorer-02 was OOMKilled twice in the evening; before each kill it logged FRD-W118 and its memory climbed, and payments-api logged PAYAPI-W0310 while the pod was slow or restarting.
title: Evening handoff: fraud-scorer-02 OOMKilled twice while redis-features lagged

# redis-sessions failover on 12 November 2025: what happened

team-identity with team-platform. sev3. 18:05 to 18:15 UTC. We followed RB-018's checks during the incident.

**What did users see?**

From 18:05 some users were asked to log in again (`AUTH-E401X`). The sessions that were lost belong to logins handled by auth-service-02 between 18:05 and 18:07:45. A smaller group, whose sessions were created through the other auth-service instance in that window, also had a lookup fail when their next request went through auth-service-02; their sessions were not lost, and logging in again fixed it. By 18:09 `AUTH-E401X` was back to its usual trickle.

**Which node was the primary?**

redis-sessions-02, since the planned failover on 7 October 2025. redis-sessions-01 was patched after that one and stayed a replica. Since this incident redis-sessions-01 is the primary again.

**Why did Sentinel fail over?**

At 18:04:30 a host-firewall rule was added by hand on redis-sessions-02 during hardening work. It dropped traffic from the two VMs that run our other Sentinels, and nothing else: auth-service pods and the replication link from redis-sessions-01 still got through. Those two Sentinels stopped getting replies, waited out the 30 s `down-after-milliseconds`, agreed at 18:05:00 (2 of 3, our quorum), and promoted redis-sessions-01 at 18:05:05. Up to that moment replication was working, so nothing written before the failover was lost.

**Why were sessions lost after that?**

redis-sessions-02 never learned it had been replaced: the Sentinels that knew couldn't reach it. It still answered as a primary. The other auth-service instance switched to redis-sessions-01 at the failover; auth-service-02 kept its connections to redis-sessions-02 and went on writing sessions there. redis-sessions-01 had stopped replicating from it, so those writes existed only on the old node. The Redis Sentinel docs describe exactly this: writes accepted by an old master that clients can still reach are discarded when it rejoins as a replica.

**Where does `READONLY` come in?**

At 18:07:40 the rule was removed. The Sentinels reached redis-sessions-02 again and at 18:07:45 reconfigured it as a replica of redis-sessions-01, which drops its own data and copies the new primary's. auth-service-02 was still pointed at it, so its next session writes got `READONLY` until 18:07:49, when it moved to the new primary. That four-second window only works because the demoted node was reachable.

**How did we confirm it was over?**

At 18:09 Sentinel named redis-sessions-01 as master, and `INFO replication` on redis-sessions-02 showed it as a replica (`role:slave`). At 18:15 the replica's offset had caught up with the primary's, and we closed it.

**What changes?**

- Host-firewall changes on the Redis VMs go through config management with a review, never by hand (team-platform).
- team-platform will look at `min-replicas-to-write` for the sessions primary. The Sentinel docs describe it as the way to stop a primary that has lost its replicas from accepting writes.
- No change to auth-service. Completing the login when the session write fails is still the right call; it is why only the next request failed and not the login itself.
resolution: The firewall change was reverted, Sentinel turned redis-sessions-02 into a replica of redis-sessions-01, and auth-service-02 moved to the new primary.
root_cause: A hand-applied host-firewall change on redis-sessions-02 cut it off from the Sentinels on other VMs, which promoted redis-sessions-01 while auth-service-02 kept writing sessions to redis-sessions-02.
symptoms: From 18:05 auth-service logged a spike of AUTH-E401X; after the failover auth-service-02 briefly got READONLY from redis-sessions-02.
title: redis-sessions failover after a host-firewall change

# Postmortem: orders-db-01 out of connection slots, 22 November 2025

Rated sev2, with times in UTC. It started at 22:15 and ended at 22:45, 30 minutes later. The database was orders-db-01.prod.internal. The runbook consulted was RB-012.

## Short version

On a Saturday night the orders database stopped accepting new sessions. The service in front of it, orders-api, could not open the connections it needed and answered with `ORD-5003`. The slots were not used up by customer traffic. A batch Job that belongs to the commerce side of orders-api, running in the `commerce` namespace, had been holding open about 222 sessions that did nothing.

## Where the 297 went

orders-db has `max_connections` of 300. Three of those are kept for superusers, which leaves 297 for application roles. Those are the slots RB-012 counts for this database.

orders-api is sized for a small share of them: three pods, each with a `pg` Pool capped at 25, so 3 x 25 = 75 at most. The rest of the arithmetic is the leak: 222 idle sessions plus those 75 come to 297, exactly the usable total. The Job had opened a new connection for every batch it processed and had never closed one, so each finished batch left a session behind in the `idle` state. Because the count is "about 222", the sum is a rounded one.

Once no slot was free, a new connection attempt was refused at login with `53300`, before any query was sent. That is why the symptom looked like a failure to connect, not a slow database. orders-api surfaced the refusals as `ORD-5003`.

## What the team saw, and what it decided

- The first sign was in orders-api: new database connections failed from 22:15.
- The query in RB-012 that lists sessions by role, application and client address is the way to see who holds the slots. The pool arithmetic showed from the outset that orders-api's own pods could account for at most 75, so the other sessions were someone else's.
- The owner of those sessions was the batch Job in `commerce`, and RB-012 asks that the owning team be consulted before idle sessions are ended, so team-commerce was brought in.
- Order of action: the Job was stopped first, so that it would stop adding to the pile; then its idle sessions were ended with `pg_terminate_backend`, after team-commerce agreed.
- The times of those two steps were not recorded. The errors had stopped by 22:45, when the incident was closed.

## Analysis

The server behaved as configured. The gap was upstream of it: a job that opened a connection per batch with no matching close, on a database whose slots are shared with the live order path.

The Job's sessions were idle, so they added no query load of their own. The budget in RB-012 had a line for orders-api but none for a batch client, so counting connections by orders-api pods alone would have looked fine.

## Gaps in the record

- Why the Job never closed its connections was not recorded.
- How long it had been accumulating sessions before 22:15 was not recorded.

## Actions proposed

1. Have the batch Job reuse one connection, or a small pool, and close it when it exits.
2. Add a warning on the count of idle sessions per client address, set well below the usable total.
3. Add the batch Job's connections to the written budget for orders-db, so the 75 is no longer the only number on the page.
resolution: The Job was stopped, then its idle sessions were ended with pg_terminate_backend once team-commerce agreed; the times of those two steps were not recorded.
root_cause: About 222 idle sessions left by an orders-api batch Job in namespace commerce, which opened a fresh connection per batch and never closed it, took the slots that orders-api's own 75 did not use, leaving none of the 297 usable ones free.
symptoms: New connections to orders-db-01 were refused with 53300 and orders-api logged ORD-5003 for 30 minutes.
title: A batch Job's forgotten sessions filled orders-db-01

# redis-cache-01 lost, 9 December 2025, early morning

sev2, 03:12 to 03:40 UTC, 28 minutes from first error to close. Runbook: RB-017.

Customers did not lose the catalog. They got it slower: for roughly 40 s the cache was unreachable, and for a while after that most product reads went to catalog-db-01 because the new primary started out nearly empty. The timeline:

**03:12** The redis-cache-01 VM is gone. Nothing on it answers and nothing tells the clients, so catalog-api calls to the cache hang and end in `ETIMEDOUT`. catalog-api begins logging `CAT-E301`, meaning it is reading from catalog-db-01 because the cache did not deliver.

**03:12:30** The Sentinels have heard nothing for the configured 30 s and agree redis-cache-01 is down. They elect and promote redis-cache-02.

**03:12:40** Clients have found redis-cache-02. From a client's side the outage was about 40 s: 30 s of waiting for the verdict and 10 s for the promotion and for clients to find the new node. `CAT-E301` stops being logged here.

**03:13** The cache on the new primary holds little. Redis normally absorbs about 95% of product reads, and those now land on catalog-db-01, whose CPU climbs and reaches about 90%.

**03:14** On-call has the incident open. A timeout, not a refusal, fits a VM that vanished. Asking the Sentinel on redis-cache-02 for the current primary gives redis-cache-02, so no manual promotion is needed and none is attempted.

**Also at 03:12** Two other services, payments-api and inventory-service, saw Redis time out as well. Each keeps its reference data in memory, reloaded every 60 s, and kept using it, so their databases got no extra reads. Those errors needed no action.

**Through the morning** The call that mattered was to wait: as popular products get cached again the hit rate rises and database CPU eases. The thing at risk was catalog-db-01, not Redis.

**03:40** catalog-db-01 CPU is back in its normal range and Sentinel points at a primary that answers. Closed.

## Open

- Why the redis-cache-01 VM was lost is not known.
- For the ticket: about 40 s unreachable, database peak near 90% CPU.
resolution: Sentinel failed over to redis-cache-02 without manual action; CAT-E301 stopped and catalog-db-01 CPU settled back to its usual range as the cache refilled, by 03:40.
root_cause: The redis-cache-01 VM was lost; Sentinel needed 30 s to mark it down before promoting redis-cache-02, and the cache then started out with little in it, so catalog reads fell through to catalog-db-01.
symptoms: From 03:12 clients saw ETIMEDOUT from redis-cache for about 40 s, catalog-api logged CAT-E301, and catalog-db-01 CPU rose to about 90%.

# #platform-oncall, Thursday 11 December 2025: inventory-db-01 root disk

Recap of the thread, grouped by who said what. 15:22 to 16:37 UTC, sev3. Runbook RB-008.

## DBA on-call

- Started the thread at 15:22. Logged into inventory-db-01.prod.internal to look at an unrelated slow query and the shell greeted them with a history-file error: no space left on device. Pasted it in the channel straight away.
- Confirmed with a database query that Postgres was answering and the inventory-service connections were still there. Asked platform to own the disk while they kept an eye on the database side.
- At 16:20, after the cleanup, re-ran their original check. Nothing on the database side looked out of place for the whole window.

## Platform on-call

- 15:26: `df -h /var` on the host, 100%. Mentioned that the log agent had been sending `ENOSPC` about its own state file for a while, which is how the problem was visible remotely at all.
- 15:34: the size breakdown of `/var` showed one dominant directory, `/var/log/journal`. Asked the channel whether anyone had changed logging on this VM recently. Nobody had.
- 15:40: `journalctl --disk-usage` agreed. Pointed out that `journald.conf` on this host had no size setting at all.
- 15:47: ran `sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=500M`. Posted the before and after free-space numbers in the thread; `/var` went from full to mostly empty.
- 15:55: added `SystemMaxUse=500M` to `/etc/systemd/journald.conf`, restarted journald, and posted the new `--disk-usage` output, now under the limit.
- 16:37: closed it after watching usage hold for a while. Total 75 minutes.

## inventory-service engineer

- Joined at 15:30 to ask whether reservations were at risk. Their dashboards showed normal error rates and latency throughout, and they did not see `ENOSPC` anywhere in the service's own logs.
- Asked whether other database VMs could be carrying the same gap. Nobody knew; that became the thread's one follow-up (below).

## Things the thread agreed on

- The database was never the problem; the root disk was, and it was full because a log store had no ceiling.
- Vacuuming through journald, rather than deleting journal files by hand, was the right call: journald keeps its own record of its files.

## Follow-up

Survey `journald.conf` across the datastore VMs to find any others without a size limit.
resolution: A journal vacuum to 500M freed the disk, and SystemMaxUse=500M was written to /etc/systemd/journald.conf on inventory-db-01 with journald restarted.
root_cause: inventory-db-01 was running without any journald size cap, so /var/log/journal kept growing on the root disk until no space was left.
symptoms: An SSH session on inventory-db-01 could not save shell history and the host's log agent reported ENOSPC; /var was at 100% while inventory-service kept working.
title: inventory-db-01 out of root disk: #platform-oncall recap

# Postmortem: card payments and the processor handshake, 19 December 2025

Severity sev1. All times UTC. Window: 21:37 to 22:47, which is 70 minutes. Runbook consulted: RB-023. Authors: team-payments.

## At a glance

On the evening of 19 December 2025 a CA rotation on the card processor's side broke the TLS handshake that card-processor-proxy makes towards the processor. `CPX-E600` marks a failed TLS handshake with the processor. From 21:37 each of the two proxy pods, card-processor-proxy-01 and -02, logged it on every outbound attempt, and payments-api returned `PAYAPI-E1107` once its 3 attempts on a payment were spent. For 70 minutes card payments could not be completed.

## Who saw what

Both pods began failing at the same minute, and the connection to the processor broke during setup each time. Identical behaviour on two independent pods pointed away from a single bad instance and away from a capacity problem, and towards something every connection to the processor had in common.

payments-api sits one step upstream. A payment that met the failing handshake on each of its attempts came back as failed. Retrying could not help, since an attempt through either pod met the same condition.

## Scope

The two proxy pods are the route from payments-api to the processor, so the failure sat on the one path that card authorisations take. The proxy is configured to make up to 3 attempts towards the processor as well, so a single payment could produce several failed handshakes before payments-api gave up on it. The rate of failed payments during the window was not recorded, so the size of the loss is not known.

## What it was not

The symptom resembles the one RB-023 covers for a lapsed client certificate of ours, and that resemblance made the runbook tempting to follow. It did not apply: our client certificate was not the problem, so a replacement from the processor was not the way out.

The rotation was on the processor's side; no detail about it is recorded. Which certificate or which verification failed is not recorded either.

## What the incident showed

A failure on the processor's side can look, from our logs, like a fault in our own TLS setup. The match with RB-023 is why a responder would first suspect our client certificate. Cause and fix for a processor-side rotation are not covered by that runbook, which is built for a lapse of our own certificate.

## How it ended

team-payments kept the incident, and card payments recovered by 22:47. The step that ended the failures was not recorded, and neither was the time at which anyone acted. No payment count for the window was kept.

## Still to settle

- How a handshake failure caused by the processor's side differs, in `CPX-E600`, from one caused by our own certificate, so the next responder can tell them apart early.
- Whether a CA rotation at the processor is announced ahead of time, and who on our side would receive that notice.
resolution: team-payments took the incident; card payments were going through again by 22:47.
root_cause: A CA rotation on the card processor's side broke the TLS handshake between card-processor-proxy and the processor; the failure did not come from our client certificate expiring.
symptoms: From 21:37 both card-processor-proxy pods logged CPX-E600 on every attempt to reach the card processor, and payments-api logged PAYAPI-E1107 once its 3 attempts were used up.
title: Card payments failed on a handshake with the processor after its CA rotation

# Handoff: catalog-api release delayed by its migration (22 December 2025)

**catalog-api-02, catalog-db-01 · release delayed · sev4 · 20:37 to 21:42 UTC · RB-028 · closed**

## Where this stands

Closed at 21:42, after 65 minutes. The catalog-api release did not go out on time: it was delayed for the whole incident. How it proceeded afterwards is not recorded.

## What happened

The release carried a database migration. A Job is a one-off task, while the Deployment is the long-running set of catalog-api pods, and migrations are not part of those pods; they run in a pre-deploy Job, `catalog-api-migrate`, and the Deployment only moves once that Job has finished successfully. Since 2025-05-16 the Job sets `PGOPTIONS='-c lock_timeout=5s'`, so a migration waits at most 5 s for a lock before it gives up.

From 20:37 the migration needed a lock on catalog-db-01 that something else was holding. It hit the 5 s limit, the Job failed and retried, and as long as the failures went on the Deployment stayed put and the release waited. catalog-api-02 is the pod named in the logs next to the Job's failures. RB-028 is the runbook for migration locks.

## Effect

The cost was the delay itself: a release that was late by the length of the incident. It is rated sev4 and carries no customer-facing error code.

## Unknowns

What held the lock on catalog-db-01 was not recorded, and neither was the number of attempts or what ended the failures.

## Next

Whoever finds the lock holder should note it in the ticket; this time it was not noted.
resolution: The catalog on-call took it at sev4 and it closed at 21:42; how the release proceeded is not recorded.
root_cause: The migration in the catalog-api-migrate Job could not get its lock on catalog-db-01 within the lock timeout, so the Job failed and retried; what held the lock is not recorded.
symptoms: The catalog-api release was delayed because its pre-deploy migration Job hit lock_timeout, failed and retried.
title: Catalog release held up by a migration lock timeout

# Ticket: 504s only when a request lands on edge-gateway-03

**Component:** edge-gateway-03.prod.internal · **Priority:** sev3 · **Span:** 21:25 to 22:25 UTC on 2026-01-16 (60 minutes) · **Playbook:** RB-014

## Symptom

Requests handled by edge-gateway-03 ended in a `504` from 21:25. Requests that the load balancer gave to the other edge pods were answered as usual, so which pod a caller reached decided the outcome. With three pods sharing the traffic, only the share landing on this one met the slow path.

## What kind of problem this is

A problem that follows a pod is a different problem from one that follows a service. The route timeout at the edge is 15 s, so a `504` here is a request that outlived that limit, and the useful question is why it did so on this pod and not on its two siblings. Had the cause been one slow service, callers of that route would have failed on all three pods. Had it been the gateway software or the node pool as a whole, the other pods would be expected to show it as well. A single affected pod with healthy siblings narrows the suspects to what is specific to that pod: the process, or the machine beneath it.

For callers the difference is practical. A retry can land on a healthy pod, so the symptom looks random from outside even though it is tied to one place, which is also why a ticket for this naming the pod is more useful than one naming a route. That is why the ticket names the pod and not a route.

## Notes from the thread

**platform on-call:** the failures follow one pod, whatever it forwards. If an upstream service were slow, its route would fail on all three edge pods. So the pod, or the machine under it, comes before any service team.

**platform on-call:** the other two pods reach the same services without trouble. RB-014 sends latency that comes from the gateway or from the node pool to team-platform, which fits the shape here although only one pod is involved.

**platform on-call:** the node under edge-gateway-03 is under resource pressure, and the gateway pod running on it is slowed by that. No figure was recorded, and the node is not named.

## Ownership and outcome

team-platform owns this, so the ticket stays with them. They took the node problem, and the `504`s had stopped by 22:25, when the ticket was closed. What was done to the node is not recorded. This ticket records no change to an upstream service or to a route, and no count of failed requests.

Pressure on the node is the only explanation on file for the slowdown on this one pod, and no measurement of that pressure is recorded either.

Follow-ups: record in the ticket which node carries the gateway pod when it is first suspected, and check the pressure on the host node as soon as a single edge pod looks slow while its siblings look fine, so the comparison with the other two pods is made early.
resolution: team-platform took the node-level problem; the 504s had stopped by 22:25.
root_cause: The node under edge-gateway-03 was under resource pressure, which slowed the gateway pod running on it; the upstream services were not the cause.
symptoms: From 21:25 requests that went through edge-gateway-03 timed out with 504 at the edge, while the other edge pods were not affected.
title: Slow requests through edge-gateway-03 while its neighbours were fine

# A feature-store restart and the minutes it spent loading, 2026-01-25

risk timeline, sev4, 01:50 to 02:00 UTC. Reference card: RB-019.

```
01:50  redis-features-01 restarts and starts reading its dataset from disk
01:50  it replies LOADING to commands that arrive during the read
01:50  fraud-scorer-01 starts logging FRD-W118 for feature lookups it cannot get answered
02:00  loading complete; LOADING replies stop and FRD-W118 ends
```

redis-features-01 is a single node with no standby, so any restart of it leaves a gap. A restarted Redis does not serve data until its snapshot is back in memory, and during that stretch it answers commands with `LOADING` instead of values. That is what the scorer's side saw: not a refusal and not a dead server, only a node that was not ready yet.

The cause of the restart was not recorded. Whether it was planned, manual or a crash is not known.

The reference card for redis-features, RB-019, is written for refused writes, which is a different state from a node that is loading. This episode did not match its main case.

The lookups affected were those fraud-scorer-01 sent to redis-features-01 between 01:50 and 02:00.

The whole episode ran 10 minutes, from the restart at 01:50 to the end of the loading at 02:00. It was sev4. No change to any setting is recorded.
