# Postmortem: month-end reconciliation crowded out the API on ledger-service-02

Severity sev2. Night of 2026-01-31 into 2026-02-01, 23:35 to 03:10 UTC. Runbook used: RB-001. Authors: ledger squad.

## Impact

For most of the night, API requests on ledger-service-02 either queued for a database connection or gave up with a Hikari message that the request had timed out after 30000ms. The effect travelled upstream: payments-api received `503` from ledger-service while the pool was starved. The incident record opens with the page at 23:35 and closes at 03:10, which is when the reconciliation batch finished. The `503` responses themselves ended earlier, in the minutes after the fix described below.

## Who was where, and what they decided

The batch had begun at 23:30. Five minutes later `LEDGER-W210` fired. Month-end has a reputation, so the first assumption was a CPU problem, and the responder opened RB-001, the runbook for a ledger-service JVM running hot. CPU on the pod was elevated but not saturated, which did not match that story, and the investigation turned to the connection pool instead.

There the picture was plain. The pool of 20 stood at 20/20 and `hikaricp_connections_pending` climbed to about 40. The connections were held by `recon-worker-*` threads, and on ledger-db-01 the 20 matching sessions were sitting in long transactions. The batch had been started with `LEDGER_RECON_PARALLELISM=24`, a higher worker count than there are connections to give them.

The decision was to shrink the batch, not the traffic and not the pool. Parallelism went from 24 to 4 and the pod running the batch was restarted so that it would read the new value. Four workers left 16 of the 20 connections to requests. The job carried on, more slowly, until 03:10. The pool size was left as it was, in line with RB-001's advice not to enlarge it mid-incident.

## Why the end time is 03:10

Responders had no clean "recovered" moment to record for the batch itself: the customer-facing `503` ended in the minutes after the restart, but the work that caused the starvation was still running and only finished at 03:10. We therefore record the end as the batch's completion, with the earlier recovery noted here in prose.

## What we take from it

- Page on pending connections, not only on pool utilisation, so a starved pool is recognised before anyone opens the CPU graph.
- Compare batch settings with the pool size whenever either one changes; 24 workers against 20 connections should not have been allowed to start.
- Add the batch's worker count to the month-end checklist, so someone reads it before the run starts.

## Open items

The write-up does not cover how long a full reconciliation takes at four workers compared with the night it ran at 24, or whether four is the right permanent number. The ledger squad should measure that at the next month-end and report it alongside the chosen setting.
resolution: LEDGER_RECON_PARALLELISM was lowered from 24 to 4 and the pod running the batch was restarted; the batch resumed with four workers and finished at 03:10.
root_cause: The month-end reconciliation ran with LEDGER_RECON_PARALLELISM=24, more workers than the pool has connections, and its recon-worker threads kept all 20 connections to ledger-db-01 inside long chunk transactions, leaving none for API requests.
symptoms: From 23:35 ledger-service-02 logged LEDGER-W210, its Hikari pool sat at 20 of 20 with up to about 40 requests pending, and payments-api received 503 from ledger-service.
title: Month-end batch workers held every ledger connection

# ledger-db-02 root disk: questions and answers

Monday 9 February 2026, 16:00 to 16:45 UTC, sev3, RB-008. Replies from the DBA lead to colleagues in finance engineering and platform.

**What tipped us off?**

A scripted probe on ledger-db-02.prod.internal stopped reporting at 16:00. Before it sends a result, it creates a scratch file; the operating system refused that file with `ENOSPC`. The resulting alert landed with the database rota.

**Did the ledger database stop serving?**

It kept going. From my laptop I issued a handful of read queries and every one came back. I'd rather not promise that every local write on that machine succeeded, because plainly some did not: the probe's scratch file is one example. My claim is narrower. Postgres logged no errors that we spotted.

**How does a database host fill up when its database hasn't grown?**

On our VMs the root filesystem also carries `/var`, and plenty besides Postgres keeps files there. `df -h /var` read 100%. A ranked listing of directories beneath it put `/var/log/journal` at the top by a huge margin.

**What made that directory balloon?**

Nothing ever limited it. `journalctl --disk-usage` matched the listing, and this machine's `/etc/systemd/journald.conf` contained no size directive. Left alone, journald retains everything it records.

**How was space recovered?**

With `journalctl --vacuum-size=500M`, which tells journald itself to discard its oldest archives until the total fits. Removing files from that directory manually is riskier, since journald keeps its own index of them. Headroom returned at 16:14.

**What keeps it from recurring here?**

At 16:21 the line `SystemMaxUse=500M` went into journald.conf, followed by a bounce of the journald service. A fresh size reading afterwards came in beneath that limit. The vacuum on its own would only have postponed a repeat.

**Where does 500M come from?**

It's our runbook's figure. Enough recent history survives for debugging, while the journal stops competing with everything else that shares this disk.

**Total elapsed time?**

45 minutes between the first failed probe and closure, mostly spent observing usage after the change to make sure it held steady.

**Any regrets?**

My opening minutes went on Postgres health, which is understandable on a ledger host but slower. Next time, `ENOSPC` from a probe on a database VM sends me to the root disk first.

**Description.** The pod behind catalog-api-02 keeps restarting. Each restart shows `OOMKilled`. The restarts come at a steady interval of about 50 minutes, not in a cluster, and the Deployment recovers each time by itself. The restarts began with the start of the window at 09:00, and the last one in the log sample came at 14:50; the ticket tracks the cause rather than each individual restart, which is why the comments below are about the pattern.

## Comments

**10:10** · catalog on-call: the pod's restart count has climbed through the morning. Its last terminated state reads `OOMKilled`, exit code 137, so the container went past its memory limit each time, rather than being stopped for some other reason. RB-005 covers the triage for this reason.

**11:00** · catalog on-call: the memory graph for catalog-api-02 since 09:00 is a straight climb, drops at each restart, and climbs again, with the restarts spaced about 50 minutes apart. The two restarts so far, at 09:50 and 10:40, are exactly that gap apart. A graph that is a straight climb is not a flat line with a peak.

**11:20** · catalog on-call: raising the limit is not the move. It would stretch the climb and push the same kill later. The limit stays as configured.

**12:15** · catalog on-call: found what grows. catalog-api keeps a cache of responses, keyed by the full query string, and there is no cap on entries. Each distinct query string becomes its own entry.

**15:20** · catalog on-call: no OOMKill since the one at 14:50. Resolving. For the record, 09:00 to 15:20 is 380 minutes; at one kill per 50 minutes that is 380 / 50 = 7.6, so about 7 restarts of this pod in the window.

## Restart pattern in the log sample

The log sample for the window shows seven kills, at 09:50, 10:40, 11:30, 12:20, 13:10, 14:00 and 14:50. Each is 50 minutes after the one before, and the first is 50 minutes after 09:00. A further one would have been due at 15:40, after the resolution. Between kills the cache entry count in the same log climbs and then starts again from small, which matches the in-process cache being lost with each restart.

## Impact

The record for this ticket covers the restarts of catalog-api-02 and nothing else. We are not describing customer-facing effects, because none were gathered.

## Notes on this ticket

This ticket does not record what change ended the restarts: no comment names a fix, and none is inferred from the cause found at 12:15. Only catalog-api-02 is called out here. Nothing in the data we looked at supports a claim about what the other catalog-api pod was doing, so none is made.

## Afterwards

- Decide on a cache key that treats equivalent requests as one entry.
- Alert on the slope of the memory graph, not only on restarts.
resolution: Handled by catalog on-call (team-catalog); no OOMKill was logged after the one at 14:50, and the ticket was resolved at 15:20. The record does not say what change stopped the kills.

# Ticket: orders-api-01 and orders-api-03 pools full, ORD-5003

**Opened:** 2026-02-28 07:05 UTC by the orders-api on-call
**Severity:** sev3
**Hosts:** orders-api-01.prod.internal, orders-api-03.prod.internal
**Runbook:** none linked
**State:** closed 08:05 UTC

## Report

Saturday, last day of the month. Requests through orders-api-01 and orders-api-03 started failing at 07:05 with `ORD-5003`. The service reads and writes orders-db through a `pg` Pool, and on these two pods the pool has no connection to give. Checking what is occupying it, and who owns it. The window is 07:05 to 08:05, so the ticket covers one hour. 

## Updates

**orders-api on-call, before the switch-off**
Pool on both pods sits at its limit of 25 (`max`). Callers wait for a free connection and give up, which is where `ORD-5003` comes from. The two pods together can hold 2 x 25 = 50 connections, and all 50 are checked out.

**orders-api on-call, before the switch-off**
The connections are held by order-summary requests, which month end makes far busier than on an ordinary day. Each one keeps its connection checked out until its own query comes back from orders-db, about 30 seconds a request. A pool of 25 hands out connections slowly when each one is gone for half a minute.

**orders-api on-call, before the switch-off**
The endpoint belongs to team-commerce, who are being asked what to do about it. Raising `max` is not being tried: a larger pool would only let more 30-second requests pile in, and it would add load on orders-db.

**07:58, team-commerce**
The order-summary endpoint was switched off.

**08:05, orders-api on-call**
Pools on orders-api-01 and orders-api-03 have drained: free connections again, no new `ORD-5003`. Closing.

## Why a 25-connection pool was enough to cause this

The pool is shared by every route on the pod. A route that holds a connection for milliseconds barely notices the limit; a route that holds one for about 30 seconds can take the whole pool by itself once enough of its requests arrive together. The month-end summary requests did that on orders-api-01 and orders-api-03, and requests on other routes then found no free connection and failed with `ORD-5003`. The summary queries ran on orders-db for their 30 seconds, which is the time each request kept its connection.

## Points worth keeping

- `ORD-5003` is orders-api reporting that a dependency call failed or timed out from its own side. Here the dependency was orders-db, reached through a pool with nothing left to lend.
- Two pods were affected, and each is counted against its own pool of 25; the figure of 50 is the two pools added, not a shared pool.
- The cause is time, not volume alone: one request holding one connection for about 30 seconds, multiplied by a month-end crowd of such requests, against a pool of 25 per pod.
- Why the summary query took about 30 seconds was not part of this ticket and is not recorded.
- When the endpoint comes back is a team-commerce call; the date was not recorded.

## Suggestion

For team-commerce and the orders-api owners: decide before the next month end how many summary requests may be in flight at once, so the pool keeps room for checkout.
resolution: team-commerce switched the order-summary endpoint off at 07:58 and the pools had drained by 08:05.
root_cause: Month-end order-summary requests each held a pg Pool connection for about 30 seconds while their query ran on orders-db, which filled the 25-connection pools on orders-api-01 and orders-api-03.
symptoms: orders-api-01 and orders-api-03 could not hand out database connections and logged ORD-5003 for an hour on the last day of February.
title: Month-end order summaries pinned the orders-api pools

# A quiet pool, then a full one: ledger-service-02 in the small hours

The incident ran from 04:40 to 05:20 UTC on 8 March 2026, forty minutes, rated sev3. It touched one ledger-service instance, ledger-service-02, and the database it talks to, ledger-db-01. This is the story as it can be told from the metrics and the logs.

It was a small-hours stretch on a Sunday, not the night of a month-end batch. RB-013 is the runbook for this Hikari pool, and it was written about a different cause.

At 04:40 `LEDGER-W210` appeared for ledger-service-02: more than ninety percent of its Hikari pool was in use. With 20 connections in the pool, that means 18 or more were checked out. Within moments none were left. From then on a caller needing the database queued, and Hikari lets a queued caller wait thirty seconds before it gives up. Each caller that reached the limit left one error line saying the request timed out after 30000ms. On the other side of the call, payments-api was getting `503` back from ledger-service.

Why would a pool of 20 stay full? Either the server hands out no more connections, or the ones in use are not coming back. The first did not apply. RB-012 holds the connection budget for ledger-db: its two ledger-service pods can hold 40 connections between them, against the 200 the database allows. The pool had its connections; they were simply occupied. On ledger-db-01, sessions from the ledger application login were working slowly through a shared statement, and every connection they sat on was one fewer for callers.

Which statement that was, and the reason it ran slowly, is not known. Nobody copied it out while it was running, so the story ends at the sessions.

The ledger on-call took the incident. By 05:20 the pool was emptying, the warnings were gone and payments-api no longer saw `503` from ledger-service. What ended the slow work is not in the record.

The incident left one practical lesson, and it is about evidence rather than settings: when the pool fills again, copy the running statements from the database into the ticket before anything else changes.
resolution: The ledger on-call took the incident at sev3; the errors stopped by 05:20.
root_cause: Slow queries on ledger-db-01 held all 20 HikariCP connections of ledger-service-02, so callers queued for the full thirty seconds; which queries ran, and why, is not known.
symptoms: From 04:40 LEDGER-W210 fired for ledger-service-02, callers hit Hikari's request timed out after 30000ms error, and payments-api got 503 from ledger-service until 05:20.
title: Slow queries kept ledger-service-02's Hikari pool full

# Search refused at the edge on 10 March 2026

I was on call for this sev3, 09:05 to 09:50 UTC. The short version is that an edge setting was too small for a day it had never been asked to handle, and the fix was a bigger number plus a restart.

**The change.** Each of the three edge pods, edge-gateway-01, edge-gateway-02 and edge-gateway-03, now lets 250 `/search` requests a second through, up from 100. That is 3 x 250 = 750 across the edge, against the 420 a second the morning's demand reached. The value sits in the edge ConfigMap, which Envoy reads at start, so it took a restart of the edge pods to apply: the change merged at 09:42 and the restart ran from 09:46 to 09:50. Refusals ended there. From the merge to the end that is 8 of the 45 minutes the incident lasted.

**What users got.** A `429` whose body carried `EDGE-RL01`. With 100 a second allowed per pod, the edge could pass 300 a second at most, so with demand near 420 about 120 a second were turned away, which is roughly 29% of searches. The first refusals came at 09:05, soon after the growth team's spring campaign began sending.

**Why it took a while.** The report said search was failing, so I looked at search-api and search-cluster first. Both were fine. The cluster was healthy and search-api's rate was flat at about 300 a second. I did not at first see that the flat figure was a ceiling set in front of it rather than the demand. RB-014 did not help directly: it is organised around slow upstreams, and nothing here was slow. What found it was filtering the edge's own access logs for `/search` and looking at the answers: `429`, on all three pods, in similar numbers each.

**After.** team-catalog looked at the cluster before the limit was raised, and agreed that it could take more.

**What did not change.** Nothing was altered in search-api or search-cluster, and no other route was touched. The setting that moved was the `/search` limit on the edge, and only that. If the edge pod count changes later, the combined limit moves with it, so the figure should be rechecked then.
resolution: The per-pod limit was raised to 250 in the edge ConfigMap and edge-gateway was restarted from 09:46 to 09:50, after which the refusals stopped.
root_cause: Each of the three edge pods allowed 100 /search requests a second, 300 in all, and the growth team's spring campaign pushed demand to about 420, so the edge refused the difference.
symptoms: From 09:05 about 120 of every 420 requests a second to /search were refused with 429 and EDGE-RL01, while search-api stayed flat at about 300 a second and search-cluster was healthy.
title: Spring campaign outgrew the edge's search limit

# Handoff: one DNS server missing a name, 2026-03-24

**internal-dns-01 and internal-dns-02, with inventory-service-01 and inventory-service-02 affected. sev3, resolved. 13:30 to 14:15 UTC. Runbook: RB-020.**

What you need to know: a config push delivered a new `prod.internal` zone file that has no entry for the inventory database. The pods go through the cluster's resolver, which caches answers briefly, so a miss from internal-dns-02 was followed by a hit once the cache had turned over.

How it went:

- 13:30 · errors start in the inventory pods. Same name each time.
- 13:40 · the datastore VMs checked and clean, so the problem was on the pod side of the path and not in the database itself.
- 13:47 · looked at the zone file on disk at each server. internal-dns-01 has the inventory database line. internal-dns-02 does not, and its copy is the newer of the two.
- 13:52 · restored the line in the zone source and pushed the corrected file to internal-dns-01.
- 13:58 · same file on internal-dns-02. Both servers now agree.
- 14:15 · no new `no such host` lines from the inventory pods. Closed.

For day shift:

1. Find out why the push stopped at one server, from the rollout run's own record.
2. Ask the owner of the zone source whether a line vanishing from a zone file can be flagged before a push goes out.
3. If a pod still errors after both servers agree, give the cluster cache a moment before restarting anything.

root_cause: A config push carried a prod.internal zone file without the inventory database record, and the new file reached internal-dns-02 alone, so the two DNS servers gave different answers.
symptoms: From 13:30 inventory-service-01 and inventory-service-02 intermittently failed to resolve their database name (NXDOMAIN, logged as no such host), while the VMs we checked kept resolving it.

# Campaign traffic overran the search cluster, 2026-04-15

search timeline, sev3, 11:05 to 11:45 UTC (40 minutes). Runbook: RB-030.

```
11:05  first SRCH-E502 on search-api-02; the queues of search-cluster-02 and
       -03 are full and both nodes are refusing queries
....   team-catalog works the incident (clock times of its steps were not kept)
11:45  no more SRCH-E502 from search-api-02
```

## Where the load came from

A growth campaign pushed people toward search. The volume exceeded what search-cluster could absorb: each node holds only so many waiting queries in its search pool, and with that queue full it declines the next arrival. search-api-02 handed that decline to its caller as `SRCH-E502`. The campaign's rate in requests per second was not measured, so the size of the overshoot was never worked out.

## The edge in this incident

The edge limit on `/search` (250 per pod, the subject of RB-030) was not what turned searches away. The searches got past the edge, arrived at search-api-02 and were declined by the cluster behind it, which is why the error is a search code and why the symptoms name a pair of cluster nodes instead of the gateway. A higher edge number would likely have sent more queries toward nodes whose queues were already full.

## Reading the timeline

Only the first and last entries carry clock times. The first is the first `SRCH-E502` seen on search-api-02, which marks the moment the cluster pools began refusing; the last is the point from which the code no longer appeared. Between them, 40 minutes passed with the pools of search-cluster-02 and search-cluster-03 full.

## Impact

The incident is sev3 and ran from 11:05 to 11:45. For forty minutes a search routed through search-api-02 could end in an error rather than a result list, because the node that received the query had no room left to queue it. The share of searches that failed and the campaign send time were not recorded.
resolution: Handled by team-catalog; refusals were over at 11:45.
root_cause: The load from a growth campaign went past search-cluster's capacity, leaving no free queue room in the pools of its second and third nodes.
symptoms: Starting at 11:05 searches through search-api-02 failed with SRCH-E502, since search-cluster-02 and search-cluster-03 had no queue space left and declined queries.
title: Campaign traffic filled two search-cluster pools

# kafka-03: root disk creeping up, Sunday night into Monday

sev4 · 2026-04-19 22:55 to 2026-04-20 00:05 UTC · broker: kafka-03.prod.internal · team-platform · runbooks: RB-008, RB-009

## Status board

| UTC | Check or action | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 22:55 | Night on-call spots disk-monitor warnings for kafka-03's `/var` in the broker's log stream | Over 90% and higher than the line before |
| 23:01 | Broker health: partitions led and followed, replication alarms quiet | Healthy, no client errors seen |
| 23:04 | RB-009 step 1, `df -h /data/kafka` on all three brokers | Similar on each, kafka-03 not an outlier: partition storage cleared |
| 23:09 | `df -h /var` on kafka-03 | Root disk above 90%, separate from partition storage |
| 23:15 | Size breakdown under `/var` | `/var/log/journal` largest; `/var/log/kafka` (GC logs) modest, rotating fine |
| 23:18 | `journalctl --disk-usage` | Agrees with the breakdown |
| 23:20 | Read `/etc/systemd/journald.conf` | Unbounded: nothing caps the journal here |
| 23:26 | Vacuum the journal to 500M | `/var` falls well below 90% |
| 23:34 | Add `SystemMaxUse=500M`, restart `systemd-journald` | Reported size below the new ceiling |
| 23:35 to 00:05 | Watch usage across midnight | Flat; incident closed at 00:05 |

Total time 70 minutes. No restart of the broker and no topic changes.

## Notes

**Order of checks.** A Kafka host has two disks that can fill, and they call for opposite responses. Partition storage under `/data/kafka` is handled with retention changes, which can discard messages a lagging consumer still needs. The root disk is handled with ordinary housekeeping. Running RB-009's opening `df` across the brokers was quick and told us which world we were in. kafka-03 sat level with its two peers, so retention stayed exactly as it was.

**Suspects on the root disk.** Two directories could plausibly have been responsible: the GC output directory the broker writes and the systemd journal. The broker's directory was small and rotating. The journal was the giant.

**Remedy.** Vacuuming released space at once. The new `SystemMaxUse=500M` line is what stops the journal climbing back.

**Who felt it.** No client errors were seen while we worked. Free space stayed above zero the whole time, so local writes kept succeeding; the warnings showed up with room to spare.

**Suggestion.** Ship the journald limit in the base image used to build VMs, so a new broker starts out bounded.
resolution: Vacuumed the journal to 500M and wrote SystemMaxUse=500M into /etc/systemd/journald.conf on kafka-03, then restarted journald; /data/kafka was not touched.
root_cause: kafka-03 had no journald size cap, so the systemd journal under /var/log/journal kept growing on the root disk.
symptoms: Disk-monitor warnings showed /var on kafka-03 above 90% and climbing late on a Sunday; the broker, its partitions and /data/kafka were all normal.
title: kafka-03 /var over 90% from journal files, data dir ruled out

# A pool-size change that did not fit the database

sev2 · 2026-04-21 · 10:05 to 10:40 UTC · cause: bad deploy · affected: inventory-db · runbook: RB-012

| Host or team | UTC | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| inventory-service-01, inventory-service-02 | 10:05 | A release of inventory-service went out with the connection pool per pod changed from 20 to 80. The pods began opening more connections to inventory-db-01 than before. |
| inventory-db-01 | 10:05 | Once the application role had used up the slots open to it, new connection attempts were refused with SQLSTATE `53300`. |
| inventory-service-01, inventory-service-02 | 10:05 | The pods saw failed connection attempts rather than slow queries, which is the mark of this class of error. |
| on-call | 10:05 to 10:40 | Compared the pools with the database's budget (below) and followed RB-012's first lever. |
| inventory-service | 10:40 | Release rolled back; pools back at 20 per pod. |
| inventory-db-01 | 10:40 | New connections accepted. Closed. |

## The numbers behind the refusals

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| max_connections on inventory-db-01 | 100 |
| Held back, outside the application's reach | 3 |
| Left for inventory-service | 100 - 3 = 97 |
| Pool before the release, two pods | 2 x 20 = 40 |
| Pool after the release, two pods | 2 x 80 = 160 |
| Wanted beyond what exists | 160 - 97 = 63 |

The old pools asked for 40 of the 97. The new ones asked for 63 more than exist, so the surplus could never succeed. The release changed one number in one service; the database saw it multiplied by two pods.

## What was decided

The rollback of the release was chosen over any change to the database. The setting on inventory-db-01 itself would have needed a restart of the server and a decision by team-dba, while undoing the release removed the demand on its own. After the rollback each pod was back to a pool of 20, and the refusals were gone by 10:40.

## Afterwards

- Check a pool-size change against the database's slot count for all pods at once, before it ships.
- Put the per-database slot figures where the release reviewer will see them.
resolution: The release was rolled back, the pools returned to 20 per pod and the refusals stopped by 10:40.
root_cause: A release raised inventory-service's connection pool from 20 to 80 per pod; two pods at 80 is 160 connections, more than the 97 slots inventory-db-01 offers to application roles.
symptoms: inventory-db-01 refused new application connections with 53300, 'remaining connection slots are reserved for roles with the SUPERUSER attribute', and inventory-service-01 and inventory-service-02 could not open all the connections they wanted.
title: Release quadrupled the pool and drained the database's slots

# On-call thread digest, Sunday 3 May 2026: feature-store writes refused

sev2, 19:25 to 20:45 UTC. fraud-scorer-01 and fraud-scorer-02 writing to redis-features-01. Grouped by what the thread dealt with, earliest first. Card: RB-019.

**Impact (from 19:25):** fraud-scorer keeps a velocity counter for each card and bumps it whenever it scores a payment. From 19:25 both scorer pods logged `FRD-E140`, the sign that those counters go stale. Both failed in the same minute, and both talk to the same single feature store, so the shared store was the obvious place to look. The counters stay stale until writes recover, so each minute of the window widened the gap between the counters and real activity.

**What the node said:** the refusal text from redis-features-01 was `OOM command not allowed`. A failed snapshot, the other route to a blocked store, gives a different error, so the cause lay in the memory limit, not in persistence.

**Why the limit bit:** memory use had reached `maxmemory 24gb`, and the store is configured with `noeviction`. Under that policy Redis answers any further write with an error rather than picking keys to discard. With only one node, nothing else could take over.

**What was weighed:** raising the cap or freeing memory were the two ways out. RB-019 allows a higher cap only if enough memory remains for the fork a background save needs, and asks that team-risk be paged before any feature key is deleted. The thread does not say which route was taken.

**Outcome (20:45, platform on-call):** writes were accepted again and `FRD-E140` had stopped on both pods. Incident rated sev2 and closed after 80 minutes, 19:25 to 20:45, with the platform on-call as owner throughout.

**Left open:**
- Which keys or settings changed to free the memory was not recorded.
- Ask team-risk which feature keys are safe to expire, so the next decision does not start from nothing.
resolution: Taken by the platform on-call; the write errors stopped by 20:45. What freed the memory is not recorded.

I was the team-payments on-call on Wednesday 6 May 2026. This sev2 ran from 02:35 to 03:10 UTC, and this is how it looked from my seat.

The page was for the `503` rate on the payment routes. In the payments-api logs the line that mattered was `PAYAPI-E1042`: a request had waited the full 500ms `DB_ACQUIRE_TIMEOUT` for a pooled database connection and been turned away. Every pod holds up to 40 connections (`pool_max_conns=40`, four pods), and on payments-api-02 and payments-api-03 all of them were in use. The pods were not short of capacity in the usual sense; the connections were simply not coming back.

My first question was whether the trouble was local to one pod or shared. It showed on both payments-api-02 and payments-api-03, so I stopped suspecting a single stuck process and went to the database. I took a goroutine dump from payments-api-02 before touching anything, for the ticket.

On payments-db-01 the sessions belonging to the payments login were mostly busy running the same statement. The pods were waiting on slow statements, and those statements kept the pool occupied. I am not naming the statement here. I did not establish why it was slow, and I would rather the ticket say so than guess.

RB-010 is the runbook for this pool-exhaustion pattern, and its mitigation is to restart after taking the dump. I restarted the payments-api pods once the dump was saved, which released every held connection. The pools drained, `PAYAPI-E1042` stopped, and by 03:10 acquire wait was back to its healthy figure of under 50 ms. I closed the incident then.

A few things about the shape of the night. Nothing about the application itself needed to change, and the pool and timeout settings stayed as they were. The only intervention was the restart, which is a bandage: the slow statements, or whatever produced them, were not addressed by anything I did.

For the review:

- Why those statements were slow. A restart clears the symptom and leaves this question open.
- Whether to alert on acquired connections per pod, so that someone hears about a filling pool before payments start returning 503.
- Whether 500ms is the right deadline: it makes a slow database visible within a second, which is good for detection and hard on customers.
resolution: The pods were restarted after a goroutine dump, which released the held connections; acquire wait and PAYAPI-E1042 were back to normal by 03:10.
root_cause: Slow statements on payments-db-01 held payments-api's pooled connections, so the 40-connection pool on each pod stayed full and new acquires ran into the deadline.
symptoms: From 02:35 payments-api logged PAYAPI-E1042 and returned 503 because pods could not get a pool connection inside the 500ms deadline; payments-api-02 and payments-api-03 had full pools.
title: Payments pool filled while the database ran slow statements

# Postmortem: payments-db-01 stopped when archiving failures filled its disk

Severity sev2. 2026-05-12, 02:20 to 05:10 UTC. Primary host: payments-db-01.prod.internal. Runbook used: RB-007. Prepared for the DBA review.

## Impact

payments-db-01 stopped serving. The data volume had no space left, the operating system reported `ENOSPC`, and Postgres shut itself down. Sessions that were connected at that moment were dropped with SQLSTATE `57P02`, the code that means the server killed them because another of its processes had crashed. With the primary gone, payments-api could not get database connections and its requests failed.

## What had gone wrong underneath

The cause was not a replication consumer and not a surge in writes. WAL archiving to object storage was failing. A WAL segment stays in `pg_wal` until the archive command has succeeded for it, so segments accumulated instead of being cleared, and the volume filled from the inside. This is the archiving branch of the payments-db WAL cases, as opposed to the stuck-slot branch.

We do not have a recorded reason for the upload failures. The review should establish what stopped the archive command working, because that is the real root cause behind this incident.

## How the night went

The incident was declared at 02:20 and closed at 05:10. The first job was to bring the primary back, which meant getting free space onto the volume and starting Postgres again. Only after the server was up did the team turn to the archiving fault, and once uploads succeeded the retained segments could be removed and disk use came down.

## Decisions and their trade-off

Service came first and understanding second. That order suited a stopped payments primary, since failed payments were piling up while the server was down, but it meant that the story of the archiving failure had to be reconstructed from logs afterwards instead of observed.

The sev2 rating reflects losing the primary of a payments service, not the size of the fault that led to it. A failing background job grew into a full outage.

## Times we can state

| Time (UTC) | Event |
|---|---|
| 02:20 | Incident start |
| 05:10 | Incident closed |

Intermediate clock times were not recorded in the ticket, so none are given here.

## Customer-facing effect

Payment requests that depended on the database failed while the primary was down. The window of the incident, 02:20 to 05:10, is the outer bound for that effect; the ticket does not record when requests began succeeding again.

## What should change

- The alert on a rising archiver failure count exists to fire well before a volume is full. The review should ask why it did not prevent this stop, and repair whichever link failed.
- The ticket should carry peak disk usage, the failing archive step and the time archiving recovered.
- If the emergency space reserve on the volume was spent, restoring it is part of closing the incident.
resolution: Space was freed, Postgres was started, the archiving fault was cleared so segments could be removed again; the incident closed at 05:10.
root_cause: WAL archiving to object storage was failing, so segments could not be removed from pg_wal and accumulated until the volume had no space left.
symptoms: payments-db-01 stopped after its data volume filled with WAL (ENOSPC); the sessions of other backends were cut off with 57P02 and payments-api could not get database connections.
title: WAL archiving failed and payments-db-01 ran out of disk

# Postmortem: a slow processor and a checkout path that kept asking

Date 2026-05-26. Window 17:05 to 17:50 UTC. Severity sev1. Proxy hosts involved: card-processor-proxy-02 and card-processor-proxy-01. Reference consulted: RB-014.

## Impact

For the length of the window customers trying to pay at checkout got an error page from the edge: `504` for about 40 mins. Behind it, payments-api logged `PAYAPI-E1107` for payments that ran out of attempts, orders-api logged `ORD-5003` for calls that failed or timed out from its side, and the proxies recorded `CPX-W429` each time the processor pushed back on one of our calls.

## What we saw, and in what order

Around 17:05 the card processor slowed down and began answering with its rate-limit reply. The first visible signs were on the proxies, with `CPX-W429` on both. The checkout path above them has two places that retry a failed call, and each is set to 3 attempts, so a single checkout could turn into as many as 9 calls toward the processor. As the processor got slower, those repeats arrived on top of the original traffic.

The page came from the edge. The on-call opened RB-014 and followed its `/checkout` row to orders-api. That was correct but one hop short of the cause: orders-api was waiting on payments-api, and payments-api on the proxy.

## Who saw what

| Team or layer | What it saw |
|---|---|
| Edge | `504` on checkout for most of the window |
| orders-api | `ORD-5003` as its payment calls failed or timed out |
| payments-api | `PAYAPI-E1107` once a payment used all its attempts |
| Proxies | `CPX-W429` replies relayed from the processor |

The processor itself allows 400 requests a second for our merchant account. Each layer saw a different symptom of the same slow dependency.

The whole window ran 45 minutes, from 17:05 to 17:50.

## Decision and result

The retries were the part we controlled. payments-api was switched to CPX_MAX_ATTEMPTS=1 so that each payment made one call toward the processor. orders-api was left as it was. Within minutes the `CPX-W429` and `PAYAPI-E1107` volume fell and the edge stopped returning `504`, and the incident closed at 17:50.

## What we do not know

The reason for the processor's slowdown is not known to us, and we have no figures for how the request rate at each hop compared during the window.

## Follow-ups

1. Put the call rate of each hop on one dashboard so the amplification can be seen directly.
2. Decide whether the checkout path should share a retry allowance between its layers.
3. Write down in the on-call notes where each layer's attempt setting lives, so the first responder can find them without searching.
4. Note in the on-call guide that a slowing processor shows up first as `CPX-W429` on the proxies.
resolution: CPX_MAX_ATTEMPTS was set to 1, which removed the retry layer closest to the processor, and the errors drained within minutes, ending the incident at 17:50.
root_cause: The card processor slowed down and pushed back on our calls; payments-api and orders-api each retried three times, so every checkout multiplied into more attempts against the processor, which kept the pushback going.
symptoms: Both card-processor-proxy pods logged CPX-W429, payments-api logged PAYAPI-E1107, orders-api logged ORD-5003, and the edge returned 504 on checkout for about 40 mins.
title: Slow card processor turned checkout retries into an edge 504 wave

# fraud-scorer-02 OOMKilled loop, 28 to 29 May 2026

sev4. UTC. Times after midnight are on 29 May. Runbook: RB-006.

```
21:52  node rotation drains the node under fraud-scorer-02; the replacement pod lands on one of the
       32-core nodes added to the general pool this month
22:00  pod Ready. WEB_CONCURRENCY is not set in the Deployment, so the entrypoint starts one gunicorn
       worker per CPU it can see: 32. The other pod, on a 16-core node, runs 16
22:11  first OOMKilled on fraud-scorer-02 (exit 137); kubelet restarts it
22:40  team-risk on-call starts on RB-006; kubectl top shows fraud-scorer-02 near its 3 GiB limit
22:48  redis-features --latency is normal and there are no feature-fetch latency warnings in the last
       hour. The cache growth RB-006 knows about needs a slow redis-features; not tonight
23:20  tracemalloc on one worker: allocations ordinary, nothing growing out of line
00:30  memory panel: fraud-scorer-02 climbs to the limit within minutes of each start; the other
       pod sits flat well below it
01:50  pgrep -P 1 on both pods: 32 worker PIDs on fraud-scorer-02, 16 on the other. Found it
02:30  WEB_CONCURRENCY=16 set in the Deployment; rollout
02:40  both pods running 16 workers
02:55  15 minutes without a kill; resolved
```

Between 22:11 and 02:30 the pod was killed about 20 times, once every 10 to 15 minutes.

## The arithmetic

A warmed-up worker holds about 150 MiB. Sixteen workers need 16 × 150 = 2,400 MiB, inside the 3,072 MiB (3 GiB) limit. Thirty-two need 4,800 MiB. The kill came once about 20 workers had warmed up (3,072 / 150 ≈ 20), which is why each start lasted about 11 minutes.

## Why RB-006 didn't point here

RB-006 is about memory growing inside each worker. Its stopgap, the `--max-requests` recycling, bounds how big one worker gets, not how many there are. Every check in it came back clean, which in the end was the clue: per-worker memory was normal, there were just twice as many workers.

## Follow-ups

- Keep `WEB_CONCURRENCY` set explicitly (now 16); never rely on the CPU-count fallback.
- Check the other Deployments whose worker or thread count comes from the visible CPU count, now that the pool mixes 16- and 32-core nodes.
resolution: WEB_CONCURRENCY=16 was set in the fraud-scorer Deployment and rolled out.
root_cause: WEB_CONCURRENCY was not set, so gunicorn started one worker per visible CPU; rescheduled onto a 32-core node, the pod ran 32 workers and needed more memory than its 3 GiB limit.
symptoms: fraud-scorer-02 was OOMKilled about 20 times overnight, each time within minutes of starting; the other pod carried the scoring traffic.
title: fraud-scorer-02 OOMKilled every few minutes on a bigger node

# Month-end reconciliation: CPU on one ledger instance

sev3 · 2026-06-01 23:35 to 2026-06-02 00:45 UTC · cause: ledger-service · affected: ledger-service-01 · runbook: RB-001

| Where | UTC | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| ledger-service-01 | 23:35 | CPU high; `LEDGER-W210` appears in its log. The month-end reconciliation had been started over HTTP, and the work of encoding its result was running on a `http-nio-*` request thread. |
| ledger-service-01 | during | The serialization kept CPU busy on that thread for as long as it ran. No clock times of the observations made in between were kept. |
| ledger-service-01 | 00:45 | CPU back to its usual level; `LEDGER-W210` no longer logged. Closed. |

## Reading the signals

**Why the warning came first.** `LEDGER-W210` fires when the share of the connection pool in use passes 90%. RB-001 lists it as an early sign when a ledger-service instance is short of CPU: threads that compete for CPU hold their connections longer, so the pool fills as a consequence. Here the warning was that consequence, and the load itself was the serialization of the reconciliation result on a `http-nio-*` request thread, a case that shows up on the single instance that took the batch.

**What it was not.** Pool exhaustion caused by reconciliation parallelism is a different problem, and the setting behind it has been at 4 since 2026-02-01. The retry threads for Kafka publishes were not what burned the CPU either.

## Context

The reconciliation runs once a month, at month end, and this occurrence began late on 1 June. It is triggered over HTTP, which is why the request thread carried the serialization. Payments traffic through ledger-service is not described for this period.

## Scope and unknowns

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Which instance | Only ledger-service-01, the one that took the reconciliation request. |
| Length | 70 minutes, from 23:35 to 00:45. |
| Size of the reconciliation payload | Not recorded. |
| What ended it | Not recorded. |

## Follow-ups

- Suggested: encode month-end reconciliation results off the request thread.
- Suggested: look at CPU on the instance that takes the request at the next month end.
resolution: Handled by the on-call; CPU on ledger-service-01 was back to normal and LEDGER-W210 had stopped by 00:45.
root_cause: Serializing the month-end reconciliation result ran on a http-nio request thread of ledger-service-01 and used its CPU; connection-pool exhaustion from reconciliation parallelism and the Kafka retry spin were not the cause.
symptoms: From 23:35 on the night of 1 to 2 June 2026 CPU on ledger-service-01 was high and LEDGER-W210 was logged.

# Ticket: 504 at the edge, orders-api-01 not answering

**Severity:** sev3
**Window:** 2026-06-09, 13:05 to 13:30 UTC
**Host:** orders-api-01.prod.internal
**Seen at:** edge-gateway
**Runbooks:** RB-014, RB-004
**State:** closed, errors stopped by 13:30

## What was reported

Slow checkout requests came back from the edge as `504`. The edge gives an upstream 15 seconds before it gives up, so each of these was a request that orders-api-01 never finished inside that time. The edge log is where the failures showed; the cause sat one hop behind it. RB-014 is the edge triage table that sends a `504` on `/checkout` to orders-api.

## What the host was doing

Node.js runs request handlers on one event loop. When a handler does synchronous crypto work, the loop is busy until that work ends, and no other handler in the process gets a turn, however many requests are waiting. From 13:05 to 13:30, which is 25 minutes, orders-api-01 was in that state. Requests queued behind the blocking work, and those that waited past the edge's limit came back as `504`, beginning within the first minute.

Seen from outside, a frozen loop looks like a slow dependency, because the waiting happens inside the process while its own calls are healthy. RB-004 describes that appearance in its memory-leak setting; it is cited here for the event-loop view only, and nothing in this ticket concerns the heap.

## Why one busy handler affects all the others

The event loop is a single thread that picks up work in turn: it reads a new request, runs a handler until the handler waits on something, resumes a handler whose reply has arrived, and writes responses back. Asynchronous calls to the database or to another service hand their waiting to the system, so the loop stays free. A synchronous crypto call does the opposite. It computes on that one thread and returns only when it finishes, and everything else in the process is held until then, including replies that have already arrived and responses that are ready to be written.

That is why the damage was not limited to the requests that triggered the crypto work. Checkouts on orders-api-01 during the window sat behind it, whichever customer they belonged to.

## Impact

Checkout requests served by orders-api-01 between 13:05 and 13:30 were slow, and those that waited the full 15 seconds failed at the edge. No count of failed checkouts or affected customers was kept.

## Times on record

| UTC | Entry |
|---|---|
| 13:05 | `504` responses begin at the edge for requests that went to orders-api-01. |
| 13:30 | Errors stopped. |

## Open

- Which code path performed the crypto work. It was not recorded.
- Whether other orders-api pods were affected. This ticket names orders-api-01 because it is the host on record.
- What stopped the blocking work.
- How many requests failed. The edge log is a sample and carries no count.

The on-call took the ticket and it was closed once the errors had stopped.

**Follow-up for the owners:** record the route and handler behind any future event-loop stall in the ticket itself.
resolution: The on-call took the ticket and the 504 responses stopped by 13:30.
root_cause: Synchronous crypto work on orders-api-01 blocked the Node.js event loop, so requests sat unanswered until the edge route timeout; which code path ran it is not recorded.
symptoms: From 13:05 edge-gateway returned 504 on checkout requests that were routed to orders-api-01, which was slow to answer.
title: Checkout 504s while orders-api-01 did synchronous crypto work

# The 13 June 2026 crawler burst on /search, as questions and answers

sev4 · 10:55 to 11:20 UTC · cause: edge-gateway limit, seen in search-api · runbook: RB-030

**What was seen?**

From 10:55 a share of `/search` requests came back from the edge as `429`, and the body of each carried `EDGE-RL01`. All three edge pods (-01, -02 and -03) logged it, so it was not one pod having a bad day.

**Who was affected?**

Anyone whose search reached a pod with an empty bucket got the refusal, crawler and ordinary users alike, because the limit does not tell them apart. Searches that arrived while a bucket had tokens were served as usual.

**Why did search-api look calm?**

The refused requests were stopped at the edge and never reached it, so search-api logged no errors of its own and saw only the traffic that was let through. Reading search-api alone would have shown a healthy service. RB-030 describes this signature from an earlier case.

**What was the limit?**

Each of the three edge pods keeps a local bucket for the `/search` route only, set to 250 requests per second per pod, which makes 3 x 250 = 750 per second across the three. When a pod's bucket is empty it answers at once and the request goes no further. Other routes have no such bucket.

**What was sending the traffic?**

A crawler. Its burst of requests to `/search` went past 250 per second on each pod. The crawler's operator, its address range and its request rate were not recorded.

**How long did it last?**

25 minutes, from 10:55 to 11:20, at sev4. Who dealt with it and what, if anything, was changed were not recorded; the refusals were gone by 11:20.

**What stayed unknown?**

How much of the refused traffic was the crawler and how much was ordinary search was not recorded, and neither was the share of refused requests.

**What would help next time?**

- Count `EDGE-RL01` responses per pod for `/search` and keep that count next to search-api's request rate.
- Decide who owns blocking a crawler at the edge, since the limit alone only caps it.
resolution: Handled by the on-call; the refusals had stopped by 11:20.
root_cause: A crawler burst on /search went past the edge limit of 250 requests per second per pod, and the edge turned away the excess.
symptoms: Between 10:55 and 11:20 requests to /search were refused at the edge with 429 and EDGE-RL01 on all three edge-gateway pods, while search-api behind them logged no errors of its own.
title: Crawler burst filled the edge's per-pod search budget

# Ticket: orders-api /checkout p99 spikes in the evenings

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Severity | sev3 |
| Service | orders-api, with orders-db |
| First seen | 2026-06-15 19:30 UTC |
| Opened | 2026-06-17 20:40 UTC |
| Closed | 2026-06-18 16:00 UTC |
| Runbooks | RB-020 (checked and ruled out) |

**Description.** Evening-only checkout slowness: the tail of `/checkout` jumps past 5 s for a minute or two at a time while the median stays normal. Orders go through; customers sit and wait. The database connection target is `orders-db-01.prod.internal`.

## Comments

**2026-06-16 09:10** · team-commerce, from alert history: on 15 June the checkout p99 alert opened and cleared five times between 19:30 and 22:00, never long enough to page. Same again last night. Put down to evening traffic.

**2026-06-17 20:40** · on-call, team-commerce: paged. Third night of the same shape.

**2026-06-17 20:55** · on-call: gateway logs for `/checkout` show every slow request finishing `200`, with nearly all of its time spent upstream in orders-api. Durations pile up a little past 5 s; a second, smaller pile sits a little past 10 s.

**2026-06-17 21:00** · platform on-call: walked RB-020 in case the database record was flapping in the `prod.internal` zone. `dig` against each internal-dns server gives identical answers and identical serials; coredns journals quiet. Ruled out.

**2026-06-17 21:10** · on-call: orders-api-01, -02 and -03 look healthy by every runtime measure: memory steady, no restarts, the event loop responsive. Something is waiting without blocking.

**2026-06-17 21:25** · on-call: from a pod, resolved the database hostname 200 times with `dns.lookup` and timed each. Nearly all answered within a few milliseconds; two needed a little over five seconds. The delay sits in name resolution.

**2026-06-17 21:40** · on-call: the pod resolver runs with `ndots:5`. Our database hostname contains only two dots, under that threshold, so glibc first tries it with each of the three cluster search suffixes and only then bare, asking for both A and AAAA records each time: 4 × 2 = 8 UDP queries per resolution. When one answer never arrives, the resolver sits out its 5 s timeout and asks again, usually with success. Two dropped answers within one resolution, on different queries, cost about 10 s while the request still succeeds. A query that loses both its attempts ends as `getaddrinfo EAI_AGAIN`: five such errors across the three nights, all for a hostname that resolves normally on demand. Why answers get dropped on this cluster is still unknown, and we are not guessing.

**2026-06-17 21:50** · on-call: the burst effect. orders-api's `pg` Pool closes connections idle longer than `idleTimeoutMillis`, left at the 10000 default. Between checkout bursts the pool empties, so each burst reconnects and each reconnect resolves the hostname again. Resolution runs on libuv's 4 worker threads, which file I/O also uses; a couple of resolutions stuck for 5 s leave the rest of the burst queued behind them.

**2026-06-17 22:15** · on-call: nothing safe to change tonight; stays sev3.

**2026-06-18 14:30** · team-commerce: reviewed change. (1) The orders-api Deployment's `dnsConfig` sets `ndots` to "2": the database hostname now goes out unsuffixed first, so one resolution is 2 queries rather than 8, a fourth as many chances to drop an answer. Shorter in-cluster names keep using the suffixes. (2) `idleTimeoutMillis` raised to 60000 so short lulls keep their connections. `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` stays as it is: extra worker threads would mask stalled lookups, not speed them up.

**2026-06-18 15:40** · team-commerce: rollout started.

**2026-06-18 16:00** · team-commerce: rollout complete on all three pods, which now resolve with `ndots:2`. Closing.
resolution: On 18 June orders-api got ndots 2 in its Deployment dnsConfig and the pg Pool idleTimeoutMillis was raised to 60000.
root_cause: Each lookup of orders-db-01.prod.internal under ndots:5 sent 8 UDP queries, and a lost reply cost a 5 s resolver timeout; the pg Pool's 10 s idle timeout made every checkout burst open new connections and repeat the lookup.
symptoms: On three evenings /checkout p99 jumped to about 5 s, with a smaller group near 10 s and a few getaddrinfo EAI_AGAIN errors; requests still succeeded.
title: orders-api checkout p99 bursts on three evenings

# Ticket: fraud-scorer writes failing against redis-features-01

**Opened:** 2026-06-17 11:35 UTC
**Severity:** sev2
**Hosts:** redis-features-01.prod.internal, fraud-scorer-01.prod.internal, fraud-scorer-02.prod.internal
**Runbook:** RB-019
**State:** closed, 13:20 UTC

## Description

Starting at 11:35 each scorer pod logged `FRD-E140`, the code for a velocity-counter write that did not go through. Each rejected write came back from redis-features-01 as `OOM command not allowed`. The failing operation was the write; the ticket records no other symptom on the node.

## Comments

**No time kept, on-call**
Both pods failed together. They share one datastore, a single Redis node with no failover partner, so redis-features-01 is the place the ticket points at.

**No time kept, on-call**
Used memory on redis-features-01 had reached its configured `maxmemory` of 24gb, and the node runs with `noeviction`. Redis picks no keys to drop under that policy and returns the error above to every further write. RB-019 is the runbook for this node.

**No time kept, team-platform**
Took over the node. The steps team-platform took on the node were not written into this ticket.

**13:20, team-platform**
Writes are accepted, and neither pod logs the code any more. Closing.

## Sequence of the ticket

| Stage | Event |
|---|---|
| Opening | Ticket opened; first refused write logged by the scorer pods |
| Middle, no time kept | Memory limit identified as the reason for the refusals; team-platform takes over the node |
| Closing | Writes accepted again; ticket closed |

## What the scorers lose

A velocity counter is a running per-card figure that fraud-scorer updates with an increment each time it scores a payment, and each counter carries an expiry. While the node refused writes, the figures the scorers would have updated stayed where they were. A counter is only as useful as its latest increment, so the refusals mean stale inputs for as long as they last, and the size of the staleness grows with the time the node stays full.

## Duration and effect

The ticket stayed open for 105 minutes, counted from its opening to the closing comment. Across that span the velocity counters could not be refreshed. fraud-scorer increments a counter for a card on every score and gives it a time-to-live, so each refused write left a counter at its last value while real activity went on. The longer the node stayed full, the further those counters fell behind.

## The machine

redis-features-01 is a 32 GB virtual machine with no swap, and Redis on it is limited to 24gb of that. That leaves 32 - 24 = 8 GB of the machine outside the Redis limit. fraud-scorer is the only client named in this ticket, and its two pods are the ones that logged the code.

## Ownership

redis-features belongs to team-platform, which also owns RB-019, so the handover to team-platform in the comments above kept the incident with the owners of the datastore. The scorer pods belong to the fraud-scoring side; their logs carry the code, and the ticket was opened at 11:35.

## Left open

- The size of the counter gap at the end was not measured.
- What the memory had been used up by is not stated anywhere in the ticket.
resolution: team-platform took the incident; writes were being accepted again and FRD-E140 had stopped by 13:20.

# Late emails on 29 June 2026 (sev4)

Owner: team-growth. Window: 17:30 to 21:10 UTC. Runbook used: RB-009.

## What customers noticed

On the evening of Monday 29 June, order confirmations and shipping emails arrived late, the worst of them about an hour late. Every email was eventually sent. Nothing else in checkout or payments was involved.

## Timeline (UTC)

- 17:30 · the email provider's API starts answering slowly; consumer lag on `notifications.outbound` begins to climb.
- 17:52 · lag passes 20,000 messages and notification-worker-01 and notification-worker-02 both log `NTF-E710`.
- 18:05 · team-growth on-call picks it up. Both pods healthy, no restarts, sends succeeding, just slowly.
- 18:30 · used RB-009's retention check: `notifications.outbound` has no retention override, so it keeps the broker default of 168 h, while lag for the `notification-worker` group was about 54,000 messages. We were minutes behind, not days. No retention change, no disk work.
- 20:30 · the provider recovers; sends are back to their usual speed.
- 20:59 · lag drops below 20,000; `NTF-E710` stops.
- 21:03 · lag reaches zero.
- 21:10 · resolved.

## Why the backlog grew

Each worker pod keeps 20 sends in flight, so the two pods have 40 going at once. At the usual 0.33 s per send that is about 120 sends a second, three times the evening arrival rate of about 40 messages a second. During the slowdown a send took about 1.6 s, so throughput fell to 40 / 1.6 = 25 a second, 15 a second short of what was arriving.

At 15 a second the backlog reached the 20,000 threshold after about 22 minutes, at 17:52. By 18:30 it was 15 × 3,600 = 54,000, which at 40 a second is roughly 23 minutes of mail. By 20:30, three hours in, it stood at about 15 × 10,800 = 162,000, a little over an hour of mail.

Once sends were fast again, the workers ran at about 120 a second against 40 arriving, so the backlog shrank by about 80 a second. Getting from 162,000 down to 20,000 took about 1,775 s, roughly 29 minutes (20:59); emptying it took about 2,025 s (21:03).

## What we did not do

We didn't add pods or raise the in-flight count: the provider was the slow part, and pushing more concurrent requests at a degraded API rarely helps. We didn't touch retention: the oldest unread message was never close to the topic's limit.

## Follow-ups

1. Alert on lag measured in minutes of traffic, not a fixed message count; 20,000 means very different delays at noon and at night.
2. Ask the provider for their incident report.
3. Add a status line to the customer support dashboard when email is running late.
resolution: The provider recovered at 20:30 and the workers drained the backlog by 21:03; nothing was changed on our side.
root_cause: The external email provider's API slowed from about 0.33 s to about 1.6 s per send, cutting notification-worker's throughput below the rate messages arrived.
symptoms: Consumer lag on notifications.outbound climbed for three hours and both notification-worker pods logged NTF-E710; order and shipping emails arrived up to about an hour late.
title: Email provider slowdown left notifications an hour behind

**00:24 risk-oncall:** quick pass through RB-006 to make sure this isn't the memory pattern dressed up as CPU. Working set flat on both, no restarts, feature fetches fast. Not that.

**00:26 risk-oncall:** so per RB-002 the pods are spending their quota early in each period, and the only thing that moved is the code. More CPU per score, same budget.

**00:27 release-captain:** options are raise the limit or go back. I'd rather not resize anything at midnight to fit a release we haven't understood.

# Two logout waves from one auth-service release

team-identity · sev2 · 2026-07-21, 14:05 to 14:30 UTC · runbooks: RB-026, RB-018

## What users went through

Twice in one afternoon signed-in users were sent back to the login page. The first wave came
from sessions created before the release, the second from sessions created while the release was
serving. Signing in again worked both times.

## What the release changed

This release altered how auth-service serializes session values kept in redis-sessions, keys
beginning `sess:`. Code from the release couldn't decode a value written by the previous build,
and the previous build couldn't decode one written by the release. When a value won't decode,
the lookup fails like any missing session would: `AUTH-E401X`, and the user goes to sign in.

We roll auth-service with stock Deployment settings, adding a pod before removing one. So for
several minutes both builds served traffic, and users whose requests hopped between builds were
signed out.

## Timeline (UTC)

- 14:05 rollout starts.
- 14:08 first pod of the release Ready. `AUTH-E401X` climbs immediately.
- 14:11 auth-service-01 and auth-service-02 both run the release. Sessions from before it can
  no longer be read.
- 14:14 paged on the `AUTH-E401X` rate.
- 14:16 Redis ruled out first, using RB-018's checks: same sessions primary as this morning, and
  auth-service had logged no failed session writes. No failover.
- 14:17 RB-026: errors started as that first pod went Ready, and this release touched stored
  session data, which is where rolling back stops being free.
- 14:20 rolled back with `kubectl rollout undo`.
- 14:23 a pod on the previous build is serving again. Users who signed in during the release
  start failing.
- 14:30 that second wave has faded; resolved.

## Why one release made two waves

Each wave was sessions written by one build meeting a reader from the other. Moving forward
stranded sessions created before 14:08. Moving back stranded those created between 14:08 and the
rollback. Rolling back didn't end anything; it changed which group of users paid.

## What was kept

The session values stayed in redis-sessions, unreadable rather than deleted: neither build could
interpret the other's. What users paid was forced sign-ins.

## Was rolling back right?

At 14:20 it felt safe. It wasn't cheaper. RB-026 asks, whenever a release changes stored data,
whether older code understands what newer code wrote. Here it did not. Had we stayed put and
shipped a build that decodes both encodings, people who signed in after 14:08 would have kept
their sessions. That build shipped one day later, 2026-07-22.

## Changes we are making

1. Release review flags any change to persisted formats: session values, cache keys, message
   bodies. Such changes ship in two steps: first a reader for both formats, later the new writer.
2. A dashboard panel splitting `AUTH-E401X` by ReplicaSet, so a glance shows whether errors sit
   on one build.
resolution: Rolled back at 14:20; the second wave, from sessions created by the release, faded by 14:30, and a build able to decode both encodings shipped on 2026-07-22.
root_cause: The auth-service release changed how session values stored under sess: in redis-sessions were encoded, and neither build could decode values written by the other.
symptoms: AUTH-E401X jumped at 14:08 when the first pod of the release turned Ready, and again from 14:23 after the rollback, on auth-service-01 and auth-service-02.
title: Session encoding change logged users out twice

# Questions and answers: the early-morning lookup slowdown, 23 July 2026

sev4. 03:00 to 06:35 UTC on 23 July 2026, a span of 215 minutes. Pods affected: notification-worker-01 and notification-worker-02. Runbook: RB-021.

**What was wrong, in one line?**

Both workers resolved names slowly, and a few lookups finished in `EAI_AGAIN`, the status that means a try-again.

**Did mail stop?**

How many sends were delayed, and whether any failed, was not counted. notification-worker hands each message to an external email provider over HTTP, with 20 sends in flight per pod, so a lookup that stalls holds up the send that needs it.

**What was behind the slow lookups?**

With the cluster default of `ndots:5` in place, a short name is expanded with the cluster's suffixes first and only then looked up as given.

**Was this particular to notification-worker?**

The default belongs to the cluster; a Deployment has to override it to escape it, and the record does not show that notification-worker did.

**Were the two pods affected alike?**

Both pods show slow lookups and `EAI_AGAIN` in their logs. If one fared worse than the other, that went unwritten, as did any gap between their first slow lookups.

**How big was the effect?**

Nobody measured it: the number of slow lookups and of `EAI_AGAIN` lines was never tallied, and the traffic at a 03:00 start is not described.

**What does the service do, and what did the slowdown touch?**

notification-worker is a consumer in the group `notification-worker`, reading the `notifications.outbound` topic and sending each message out through the email provider's HTTP API. Two pods share that work. The slowdown touched the name lookups on those pods; the record names no other service as affected, and the topic and its group are not recorded as having a problem of their own.

**How long did it last?**

The incident record starts at 03:00 and ends at 06:35, which is 215 minutes. Nothing between those times is dated.

**Who dealt with it, and when did it end?**

The engineer on call handled it, and lookups were normal again at 06:35. The step that ended the problem is unrecorded.
resolution: The on-call took the incident, and lookups were back to normal by 06:35.
root_cause: The notification-worker pods use the cluster default of ndots:5, so lookups of names with fewer than five dots go through the search list before the name as written; the extra queries slowed lookups and let some of them end in EAI_AGAIN.
symptoms: From 03:00 name lookups on notification-worker-01 and notification-worker-02 were slow, and some failed outright with EAI_AGAIN.
title: Slow lookups and EAI_AGAIN on notification-worker pods before dawn

# Q&A: the orders-api pool incident of 8 August 2026

sev2 · 10:15 to 10:40 UTC · cause: orders-db, seen in orders-api · runbook: none linked

**Where did it hurt?**

On orders-api-02 and orders-api-03. Each pod's `pg` Pool allows 25 connections; between them the pair could have 50 out at the same moment. Once those were all in use, requests that needed the database logged `ORD-5003` instead of being served.

**What was holding the connections?**

A slow query on orders-db. A pooled connection stays lent out while its query runs and comes back only with the answer, so while the query lasted, requests behind the busy connections queued. The query's identity and the cause of its slowness never made it into the record.

**Why only two pods?**

That is not known. The service runs more pods, but nothing was recorded about them for this window.

**Was the database out of connection slots?**

The arithmetic says it was not. orders-api runs three pods with 25 connections each, so its pools together reach 75 at most, and orders-db allows 300 connections. The trouble sat in how long each connection was held, not in how many could be opened.

**What ended the slow query?**

That was not recorded either, so the write-up stops at the moment the errors stopped.

**Were the pool settings touched?**

No change to pool settings is recorded for the window.

**How long did it last?**

From 10:15 to 10:40, which is 25 minutes. The on-call took it, and the errors were gone by 10:40.

**What did the logs show, in order?**

Pool usage on the two pods rose to its ceiling of 25 first. Only after that did requests start failing with `ORD-5003`, and the failures continued while the pools stayed full. Once the incident ended, usage returned to its ordinary range. The log lines are a sample of what the pods wrote, so they carry no failure count.

**What would have helped?**

A recorded name for the slow query. Without it, the same pattern on another day would start from the same blank.

**Open items**

- Find the query in the database's own statistics and write down why it ran long.
- Consider a gauge on pool usage that pages ahead of the first `ORD-5003`.
resolution: The on-call took the incident; the errors stopped by 10:40.

# search-cluster-01, Sunday 9 August 2026: clock log from search on-call

sev4. Runbook RB-008. Host search-cluster-01.prod.internal. All times UTC.

**00:50** Queue sweep turns up a `/var` warning on search-cluster-01. This check raises a ticket at 90%, never a page, which is why it came to me by reading rather than by a phone buzzing. The reading has crept higher since it was raised.

**00:53** Is search hurting? Queries against `products` through `search-cluster-01.prod.internal:9200` come back at their usual pace. Shards sit on a separate volume, so a crowded root filesystem threatens logging and the OS long before it threatens the index.

**00:58** Root filesystem: 40 GB, the standard size. Ordinarily about 11 GB of it is occupied. At this moment, more than nine tenths.

**01:02** Hunch: OpenSearch's log folder. One of its files once went unrotated on this cluster and swallowed a node, so that's where I look.

**01:07** Hunch wrong. `/etc/logrotate.d/` has its OpenSearch entry, live files are tiny, and compressed archives are few.

**01:12** Step back and measure everything in `/var` using `du`. Biggest by far: the systemd journal directory.

**01:16** journald's own size report matches. Its config file holds no size directive whatsoever.

**01:21** Any deleted-but-open files? `lsof +L1` lists none. The journal is the only thing to trim.

**01:24** Vacuum the journal down to 500M; journald drops its oldest archives first.

**01:26** Occupied space falls back to roughly the normal 11 GB. The next check clears the ticket condition.

**01:34** `SystemMaxUse=500M` goes into `/etc/systemd/journald.conf` under `[Journal]`; journald gets restarted. Its reported size now stays beneath that ceiling.

**01:40** Glance at OpenSearch output on search-cluster-01 to confirm the journald restart disturbed nothing. Lines flowing as normal.

**02:00** Flat. Holding it open longer, since the original climb was gradual and one reading proves little.

**02:25** Still flat. Done, 95 minutes after I picked it up.

**For daytime**

- One lesson rather than a to-do list: chasing last time's culprit first cost a few minutes. Measure all of `/var`, then follow the largest directory.
resolution: Vacuumed the journal to 500M and set SystemMaxUse=500M in /etc/systemd/journald.conf on search-cluster-01, then restarted journald; /var returned to about 11 GB used.
root_cause: search-cluster-01 had no journald size limit, so the systemd journal under /var/log/journal grew until it held most of the 40 GB root disk.
symptoms: A /var-over-90% ticket for search-cluster-01 was rising after midnight; OpenSearch logs were rotating normally and search kept working.

# Tuesday 11 August 2026, the early hours: a feature store with no room left

`OOM command not allowed` was the reply redis-features-01 gave to a write from fraud-scorer-01 at 04:10, and fraud-scorer-02 received the same reply shortly after. Each scorer logged it under `FRD-E140`. This sev3 ran from 04:10 to 06:05 UTC, and the platform on-call had it throughout.

What that wording rules out is a node that is down. redis-features-01 was up and answering; it was declining to store anything new. The configuration explains why. Its `maxmemory` is 24gb and its policy is `noeviction`, so when the data hits that size Redis selects no keys to discard; every write is answered with the error until something changes. A store built never to forget keys acts this way once it fills. RB-019 covers this datastore.

The cost sits with the scorers. Scoring a payment bumps a counter for the card, and while writes fail the per-card figures drift away from real activity. The counters carry an expiry, so old values are not meant to linger forever, yet nothing new could be stored in the meantime. Only one machine hosts redis-features and nothing stands by for it, which ruled out shifting traffic elsewhere. The two scorer pods failing in one minute against the same node made the suspect obvious, and it was not either scorer.

The logs could not say what had filled the node, and which keys were responsible was left for later. What brought the errors to an end was not written down, so no sequence is given here. The outcome is recorded: both scorer pods stopped logging `FRD-E140`, and the incident closed at 06:05.

The whole thing lasted 115 minutes, from 04:10 to 06:05. A node set to refuse rather than evict goes on refusing while its memory stays full, and the early hour changed nothing about that. Nothing in the records says how full the node was beyond the fact that it sat at its ceiling, or how quickly it had got there, and no other host is involved: the two scorer pods and redis-features-01 are the whole picture.
resolution: The platform on-call handled it; the errors were gone by 06:05 and what ended them was not noted.
root_cause: Stored data on redis-features-01 had reached the ceiling set by maxmemory, 24gb, and under noeviction Redis turns writes away at that point instead of discarding anything.
symptoms: Starting at 04:10 the two fraud-scorer pods could not update their velocity counters, each failing with FRD-E140 while redis-features-01 replied OOM command not allowed.

# Two Kafka brokers refused a pushed config

sev2 · 2026-08-13 · 10:12 to 10:36 UTC · cause: kafka · affected: ledger-service, orders-api · runbook: RB-027

| Host or team | UTC | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| kafka-01 | 10:12 | Picked as the canary. The tool replaced `server.properties`, restarted the broker and got exit code 0. A few seconds later the JVM quit with a `ConfigException` naming `message.max.bytes`. |
| whole cluster | 10:13 | Two healthy brokers remained, so each partition kept a second in-sync copy and producers carried on. No page yet: under-replication has to persist ten minutes before anyone is woken. |
| kafka-02 | 10:17 | Its five-minute pause over, the tool repeated the same steps on the next broker, with the same result. |
| producers | 10:17 | One surviving broker cannot provide two in-sync copies (`min.insync.replicas=2`), so every write asking for `acks=all` was rejected. |
| ledger-service | 10:17 | `LEDGER-E455` logged once per ledger entry that could not go out; entries moved to its retry queue and were retried with growing pauses. |
| on-call | 10:19 | Paged for producer failures. |
| on-call | 10:20 | Halted the run. The remaining broker would have been touched at 10:22. |
| kafka-01, kafka-02 | 10:25 | Last known-good `server.properties` pushed back to just these two; brokers started by hand. |
| whole cluster | 10:27 | Both brokers serving; producers succeed again. |
| ledger-service | 10:28 | Retry queue empty. |
| whole cluster | 10:36 | Every partition fully replicated. Closed. |

## Notes

**The bad value.** Kafka parses `message.max.bytes` as an integer count of bytes. Whoever wrote the change wanted roughly ten megabytes and typed `message.max.bytes=10MB`; the parser refuses the suffix and the broker aborts during startup. Ten mebibytes written correctly is 10485760.

**Why the tool saw success.** systemd treats our broker unit as up the instant its process is spawned, so a restart returns 0 even when the JVM is about to abort on its configuration. In August the tool trusted that return code alone, paused for a fixed time and moved on; nothing asked whether a broker had actually rejoined the cluster. Two brokers were gone before a human was involved.

**Effect on each Kafka user.**

| Service | Effect |
|---|---|
| ledger-service | Published nothing for ten minutes and lost nothing. Its retry queue peaked at about 1,200 entries and was empty by 10:28. CPU unchanged. |
| orders-api | Customers could check out the whole time. Order events go to the outbox first; publishing paused, then resumed with a backlog of about 2,400 events and caught up. |
| notification-worker | Idle: with no new messages arriving, it had nothing to fall behind on. |

## Follow-ups

- team-platform: health-check each broker after its push, so a config run halts on the first broker that does not come back.
- Change review: byte-valued Kafka settings must be bare integers; add a lint for unit suffixes.
- On-call note: a halted run is never resumed as-is; the corrected file goes out as a fresh run.
resolution: The run was stopped before the third broker, the previous server.properties was pushed to kafka-01 and kafka-02, and both were started; all replicas were back in sync at 10:36.
root_cause: The rollout tool pushed message.max.bytes=10MB to server.properties; Kafka needs a plain byte count, so each broker refused the file at startup while systemctl restart still exited 0.
symptoms: kafka-01 and kafka-02 exited at startup after a config push; with one broker left, acks=all producers failed and ledger-service queued entries with LEDGER-E455.
title: Pushed Kafka config stopped two brokers
